items.title: What is Repo Rate? Meaning, How RBI Uses It, Example
items.description: Repo rate is the rate at which RBI lends overnight to banks against government securities. Learn how it works, why it moves loan EMIs, with an example.
items.short: Repo rate is the interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends short-term money to banks, which pledge government securities as collateral and buy them back later.
body: 'Repo' is short for repurchase agreement. A bank that needs funds sells eligible government securities to RBI and agrees to buy them back the next day (or after a few days) at a slightly higher price. The difference between the two prices, expressed as an annual percentage, is the repo rate.

The repo rate is RBI's policy rate, the single number that signals the stance of monetary policy. It is fixed by the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which meets at least four times a year (usually six). When the MPC raises the repo rate, borrowing from RBI becomes costlier, banks raise their own lending and deposit rates, credit growth slows and demand cools, which helps control inflation. A cut does the opposite and supports growth.

Since October 2019, banks must link floating-rate retail and MSE loans to an external benchmark, and most banks chose the repo rate. So a repo change now passes to home-loan EMIs within one reset period instead of months later. The repo rate also anchors the liquidity corridor: the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) sits below it and the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) above it.

A common confusion in bank exams is the direction of money. Under repo, RBI gives money to banks; under reverse repo, banks park money with RBI. Another trap: the repo rate is not the rate you pay on a loan. Your bank adds a spread (for credit risk and costs) on top of it. The current figure changes with each policy review, so always check the latest RBI monetary policy statement (as of 2026).
items.example: Suppose the repo rate is 5.50% and a bank sells securities worth ₹1,000 crore to RBI for one day. Interest = 1,000 × 5.50% × 1/365 = about ₹0.15 crore (₹15.07 lakh). The bank buys the securities back next day for roughly ₹1,000.15 crore. If a home loan is priced at repo + 2.75%, it would carry 8.25%. If the MPC cuts repo by 0.25%, the loan rate falls to 8.00% at the next reset.
faqs: Who decides the repo rate in India?

The Monetary Policy Committee constituted under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act decides the repo rate by majority vote. It has three RBI members including the Governor and three external members appointed by the Central Government. If votes are tied, the Governor has a casting vote. RBI then implements the decision through its liquidity operations.
Does a repo rate cut immediately reduce my loan EMI?

Only for loans linked to the repo rate, and only at the next reset date, which must be at least once every three months under external benchmark rules. Loans on older MCLR or base rate systems adjust more slowly. Many banks also keep the EMI unchanged and shorten the tenure instead, so check your loan statement.

items.title: Reverse Repo Rate Meaning: How It Differs from Repo
items.description: Reverse repo rate is what RBI pays banks for parking surplus funds against securities. See how it differs from repo and SDF, with a worked example.
items.short: Reverse repo rate is the interest rate RBI pays banks when they lend surplus money to RBI and receive government securities as collateral in return.
body: Reverse repo is the mirror image of repo. When banks have more cash than they need, they can lend it to RBI. RBI gives them government securities as collateral and pays interest at the reverse repo rate. The tool absorbs excess liquidity from the banking system, so it is called a liquidity-absorption window.

For many years the reverse repo rate was the floor of RBI's interest-rate corridor, with a fixed gap below the repo rate. A limitation was that RBI needed enough government securities to hand over as collateral. In April 2022 RBI introduced the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), which absorbs funds without collateral, and made SDF the new floor. The fixed-rate reverse repo still exists on paper but is now a secondary tool used at RBI's discretion; RBI also runs variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions to drain surplus liquidity.

Why does it matter for exams? Questions often ask which rate absorbs liquidity (reverse repo, SDF) and which injects it (repo, MSF). Older study material may say 'reverse repo is the floor of the LAF corridor'. That was true before April 2022, but for current-affairs papers like RBI Grade B, the SDF rate is the floor. Since the fixed reverse repo rate has not been revised alongside the policy rate for a long time, verify the figure in the latest RBI statement (as of 2026).

A common mistake is to think a high reverse repo rate is good for borrowers. It is the opposite: an attractive rate for parking money with RBI makes banks less eager to lend to customers at low rates.
items.example: Say a bank has ₹500 crore idle at the end of the day. It parks the money with RBI under a 14-day VRRR auction at a cut-off of 5.20%. Interest earned = 500 × 5.20% × 14/365 = about ₹0.997 crore, roughly ₹99.7 lakh. If instead it uses the overnight SDF window at 5.25%, it earns 500 × 5.25%/365 = about ₹7.19 lakh for one night, without RBI needing to give it securities.
faqs: Is reverse repo rate always lower than repo rate?

Yes. RBI pays banks less for parking money than it charges them for borrowing, otherwise banks could borrow and re-lend to RBI for a riskless profit. The spread between the two has changed over time, and since 2022 the SDF rate, not the fixed reverse repo rate, sits just below repo as the corridor floor.
What is variable rate reverse repo (VRRR)?

VRRR is an auction in which banks bid the interest rate at which they will park surplus funds with RBI for a fixed term, such as 7 or 14 days. RBI decides the amount to absorb, and the cut-off rate comes from the bids. It lets RBI drain large, lasting surpluses more flexibly than the overnight windows.

items.title: Standing Deposit Facility (SDF): Meaning and Rate
items.description: SDF lets banks park surplus funds with RBI overnight without collateral. Learn why RBI introduced it in 2022, its link to repo rate and why it is the floor.
items.short: The Standing Deposit Facility is an RBI window where banks deposit surplus funds, usually overnight, and earn interest without receiving any collateral from RBI.
body: RBI introduced the SDF in April 2022 using powers under Section 17 of the RBI Act, as amended in 2018. The idea had been recommended by the Urjit Patel committee in 2014. Unlike reverse repo, RBI does not have to give the bank government securities in return, so RBI can absorb any amount of surplus money even when its own stock of securities is limited.

The SDF rate is set at 25 basis points below the repo rate and acts as the floor of the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) corridor. The MSF rate, 25 basis points above repo, is the ceiling. Because the floor moves automatically with the repo rate, every policy rate change shifts the whole corridor. The width and the spreads can be revised by RBI, so confirm current figures (as of 2026).

Banks use SDF at the end of the day when they have cash left after meeting their cash reserve ratio and other needs. Balances kept under SDF are not counted towards CRR, but RBI has allowed them to be counted as an eligible asset for the liquidity coverage ratio. The window is available every day, including weekends and holidays, and banks can access it at their discretion, which is what 'standing' means.

The key exam point is the purpose: SDF is a liquidity absorption tool, not a lending tool. It also helps keep the overnight call money rate (the weighted average call rate, RBI's operating target) from falling too far below the repo rate when liquidity is in surplus.
items.example: Assume repo is 5.50%, so SDF is 5.25% and MSF is 5.75%. A bank with ₹2,000 crore surplus on a Friday parks it under SDF until Monday (3 days). Interest = 2,000 × 5.25% × 3/365 = about ₹0.863 crore, or roughly ₹86.3 lakh. RBI gives no securities in return; the bank's deposit is simply credited back with interest on Monday.
faqs: Why did RBI need SDF when reverse repo already existed?

Reverse repo needs RBI to hand over government securities as collateral. During the large liquidity surplus after 2020, absorbing huge sums that way strained RBI's stock of securities. SDF removes the collateral requirement, so RBI can absorb surplus money without limit and without disturbing its balance sheet holdings of bonds.
Is SDF the same as a fixed deposit with RBI?

Loosely, yes, but only banks and other eligible institutions can use it, and it is mainly overnight. Individuals cannot deposit with RBI under SDF. The rate is tied to the repo rate rather than negotiated, and the balance is not counted towards the bank's cash reserve ratio.

items.title: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) Meaning with Example
items.description: MSF is RBI's emergency overnight window where banks borrow above the repo rate, even dipping into SLR securities. Know the rate, limit and purpose here.
items.short: Marginal Standing Facility is an emergency window through which scheduled banks borrow overnight from RBI at a rate above repo, pledging government securities, including some held for SLR.
body: RBI introduced MSF in May 2011 as a safety valve. Normal repo funding is limited and offered through auctions, so a bank facing a sudden, unexpected cash shortage at the end of the day needs somewhere to go. Under MSF it can borrow overnight without waiting for an auction, but at a penalty rate, currently set at 25 basis points above the repo rate (check the latest RBI statement as of 2026).

The special feature is that banks may dip into their Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) holdings. Normally securities held for SLR cannot be pledged, but under MSF a bank can use them up to a limit set by RBI, expressed as a percentage of its net demand and time liabilities (NDTL). This limit has been 2% of NDTL for most of the facility's life and was temporarily raised during the pandemic.

The MSF rate is the ceiling of the liquidity adjustment facility corridor; the SDF rate is the floor and the repo rate sits in the middle. Since 2014 the Bank Rate has been aligned with the MSF rate, so the two always move together.

Exam traps: MSF is for scheduled commercial banks (and some others RBI permits), not NBFCs; it is overnight, not term borrowing; and it injects liquidity, unlike SDF. Heavy use of MSF by banks is read as a sign of tight liquidity in the system.
items.example: A bank's NDTL is ₹1,00,000 crore. With a 2% dip-down limit it can pledge SLR securities worth up to ₹2,000 crore under MSF. If repo is 5.50%, MSF is 5.75%. Borrowing ₹1,500 crore overnight costs 1,500 × 5.75%/365 = about ₹0.236 crore, or ₹23.6 lakh, compared with about ₹22.6 lakh at repo. The extra ₹1 lakh is the price of emergency access.
faqs: What is the difference between MSF and repo?

Repo funds are offered by RBI, often through auctions, at the policy rate, and banks must pledge securities in excess of their SLR requirement. MSF is available on demand at a higher rate, and banks can pledge securities from their SLR portfolio up to a set limit. MSF is the last-resort window; repo is routine funding.
Can a bank breach SLR by using MSF?

Technically its SLR holding falls below the required level, but RBI permits this within the MSF dip-down limit, so it is not treated as a default. Borrowing beyond the permitted dip-down would be a genuine SLR shortfall and attract penal interest under the Banking Regulation Act.

items.title: What is Bank Rate? Meaning and Difference from Repo
items.description: Bank rate is the standard rate at which RBI buys or rediscounts bills, under Section 49 of the RBI Act. See why it equals MSF today and where it is used.
items.short: Bank rate is the standard rate at which the Reserve Bank of India is prepared to buy or rediscount bills of exchange and other commercial paper, as defined in Section 49 of the RBI Act.
body: Bank rate is one of the oldest instruments of monetary policy. In earlier decades, before repo operations, RBI used it as the main signal: a higher bank rate made long-term refinance costlier and tightened credit. The rate is published under Section 49 of the RBI Act, 1934.

With the introduction of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility in 2000 and the repo rate's rise as the policy rate, bank rate lost its signalling role. Today RBI keeps it aligned with the Marginal Standing Facility rate, so when MPC changes the repo rate, MSF and bank rate move automatically by the same amount. It is no longer an independent policy decision.

Why learn it then? Bank rate is still used as a reference in several rules. Penal interest that RBI charges banks for shortfalls in maintaining CRR or SLR is linked to the bank rate, for example bank rate plus 3% at first, rising to bank rate plus 5% if the shortfall continues. Some statutes and contracts also cite 'bank rate' when fixing interest on delayed payments.

The classic difference: repo is a short-term loan against securities (a repurchase deal), while bank rate refers to rediscounting of bills or long-term lending without a repurchase agreement. In current exams, if asked 'which rate is equal to MSF', the answer is bank rate.
items.example: Say repo is 5.50%, so MSF and bank rate are 5.75%. A bank falls short of its required CRR by ₹100 crore for one day. Penal interest at bank rate + 3% = 8.75%. Charge = 100 × 8.75%/365 = about ₹0.024 crore, roughly ₹2.40 lakh for that day. If the shortfall continues and the rate rises to bank rate + 5% (10.75%), the daily cost goes up to about ₹2.95 lakh.
faqs: Is bank rate the same as the rate banks charge customers?

No. Despite the name, bank rate is the rate RBI uses, not a rate banks charge borrowers. Your loan rate depends on the bank's benchmark, such as the repo-linked rate or MCLR, plus a spread. Bank rate today mostly matters as a reference for penal charges and in some legal provisions.
Under which section of the RBI Act is bank rate defined?

Section 49 of the RBI Act, 1934 requires RBI to make public the standard rate at which it is prepared to buy or rediscount bills of exchange or other commercial paper eligible for purchase under the Act. This published standard rate is the bank rate.

items.title: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) Meaning, Formula and Example
items.description: CRR is the share of a bank's net demand and time liabilities kept as cash with RBI, earning no interest. Learn the formula, NDTL and a worked example.
items.short: Cash Reserve Ratio is the percentage of a bank's net demand and time liabilities that it must keep as a cash balance with RBI, on which RBI pays no interest.
body: CRR is prescribed under Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934 for scheduled banks. It is calculated on net demand and time liabilities (NDTL), which broadly means customer deposits (savings, current, fixed) plus certain other liabilities, minus specific exempted items such as inter-bank liabilities. Banks report NDTL fortnightly, and CRR is maintained on an average daily basis, with a minimum of 90% of the requirement on every single day.

Because the money sits idle with RBI, CRR is both a safety cushion and a monetary policy lever. Raising CRR locks up more cash and reduces what banks can lend, which drains liquidity. Cutting CRR frees money for lending. A CRR change affects liquidity directly and in large amounts, so RBI uses it sparingly compared with the repo rate. RBI cut CRR in phases during 2025 to 3% of NDTL; check the current figure in the latest monetary policy statement (as of 2026).

CRR differs from SLR in three ways that exams love: CRR is kept with RBI, SLR is kept by the bank itself; CRR is in cash only, SLR can be cash, gold or approved securities; and CRR earns nothing, while SLR securities earn interest.
A shortfall attracts penal interest linked to the bank rate. Because CRR earns nothing, it acts like a tax on deposits, which is one reason banks lobby for lower CRR.
items.example: A bank's NDTL is ₹2,00,000 crore and CRR is 3%. Required CRR balance = 2,00,000 × 3% = ₹6,000 crore, kept with RBI. If RBI cuts CRR by 0.50 percentage point to 2.5%, the requirement falls to ₹5,000 crore, freeing ₹1,000 crore. At an 8% lending rate, that freed cash could earn the bank about ₹80 crore a year.
faqs: Does RBI pay interest on CRR balances?

No. Since 2007 RBI pays no interest on CRR balances, after the RBI Act was amended to remove the floor and ceiling on CRR along with the interest obligation. This is why CRR is costly for banks and why any cut directly improves their earning capacity.
What is NDTL in CRR calculation?

Net demand and time liabilities is a bank's demand liabilities (current and savings deposits, demand drafts outstanding) plus time liabilities (fixed deposits, recurring deposits), plus other liabilities, minus specified exemptions like inter-bank liabilities. CRR and SLR are both calculated as a percentage of NDTL.

items.title: Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): Meaning and Example
items.description: SLR is the share of NDTL that banks must hold in cash, gold or approved government securities. See how SLR differs from CRR and why it matters for banks.
items.short: Statutory Liquidity Ratio is the minimum share of net demand and time liabilities that a bank must hold in liquid assets: cash, gold, or unencumbered approved government securities.
body: SLR is prescribed under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Unlike CRR, the assets stay with the bank. In practice almost all SLR holdings are government securities: central government bonds, treasury bills, and state development loans. The ceiling under the Act is 40% of NDTL; RBI has kept it at 18% since 2020 (check the current figure as of 2026).

SLR serves two purposes. First, it ensures solvency and liquidity: if depositors suddenly withdraw, the bank has assets that can be sold or pledged quickly. Second, it creates a captive demand for government bonds, which helps the government borrow. Critics call this financial repression because it pushes banks to hold bonds even when private lending would earn more.

Changes in SLR are now rare and are not used for routine monetary policy. However, SLR securities interact with other tools: under the Marginal Standing Facility, banks may dip into SLR holdings up to a limit. Securities in excess of the SLR requirement are what banks pledge for repo borrowing.

Remember the differences from CRR: SLR assets earn interest, are held by the bank itself, and can be in three forms, while CRR is only cash parked with RBI. The 'unencumbered' condition matters: securities already pledged elsewhere cannot be counted.
items.example: A bank with NDTL of ₹1,50,000 crore and an 18% SLR must hold ₹27,000 crore in eligible assets. If it holds ₹30,000 crore of government securities, ₹3,000 crore is excess SLR, which it can pledge for repo. If these bonds yield 6.8%, the SLR portfolio earns about 27,000 × 6.8% = ₹1,836 crore a year, unlike CRR money which earns nothing.
faqs: Is SLR maintained with RBI?

No. SLR assets are maintained by the bank itself, in its own vaults or in its securities account (SGL account with RBI for government bonds). The bank owns and earns interest on them. Only CRR is a cash balance with RBI. This is one of the most frequently tested differences.
Can SLR and LCR overlap?

Yes. Government securities held for SLR can also count as high-quality liquid assets for the liquidity coverage ratio, within limits RBI allows, such as the MSF dip-down portion and a further 'FALLCR' carve-out. So the same bond can partly serve both requirements.

items.title: Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) and the RBI Corridor
items.description: LAF is RBI's framework of repo, reverse repo, SDF and MSF used to manage daily bank liquidity. Learn the corridor, the operating target and an example.
items.short: Liquidity Adjustment Facility is RBI's framework of operations, mainly repo and reverse repo-type windows, used to inject or absorb liquidity in the banking system day to day.
body: RBI introduced the LAF in June 2000 on the recommendation of the Narasimham Committee (1998). Before that, liquidity was managed mainly through CRR changes and refinance. LAF made the repo rate the main policy rate and allowed RBI to fine-tune liquidity every day.

Today LAF has standing facilities and market operations. Standing facilities are available on demand: the Standing Deposit Facility (floor) and the Marginal Standing Facility (ceiling). Market operations include fixed-rate repo, variable rate repo (VRR) auctions to inject funds and variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions to absorb funds. The repo rate sits in the middle of the corridor.

RBI's operating target is the weighted average call rate (WACR), the rate at which banks lend to each other overnight. RBI tries to keep WACR close to the repo rate. If liquidity is in surplus, WACR falls towards the SDF floor, and RBI runs VRRR auctions. If liquidity is in deficit, WACR rises towards the MSF ceiling, and RBI injects funds through VRR auctions or open market purchases.

Liquidity has two kinds of drivers. Frictional changes, such as tax payments or festival cash withdrawals, are handled through LAF. Durable changes, such as large foreign exchange inflows, are handled through open market operations, CRR changes or forex swaps. Exams often ask which tool fits which situation.
items.example: Suppose repo is 5.50%, SDF 5.25% and MSF 5.75%, so the corridor is 50 basis points wide. In mid-March, advance tax payments move about ₹1.5 lakh crore from bank accounts to the government's account with RBI. Banks run short, and WACR climbs to 5.70%. RBI announces a 7-day VRR auction of ₹1 lakh crore; banks borrow, and WACR settles back near 5.50%.
faqs: What is the LAF corridor?

It is the band between the SDF rate (floor) and the MSF rate (ceiling), with the repo rate in the middle. Overnight market rates are expected to stay inside it because banks will not lend below what RBI pays them, nor borrow above what RBI charges. The width is set by RBI and has typically been 50 basis points.
Who can participate in LAF?

Scheduled commercial banks (except RRBs), and certain other eligible entities such as scheduled urban co-operative and state co-operative banks, standalone primary dealers for some windows, as permitted by RBI. Individuals and ordinary NBFCs cannot directly access LAF.

items.title: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): Members and Role
items.description: The MPC sets India's repo rate to meet the CPI inflation target. Learn its six members, quorum, voting, the 4% target and the 2% to 6% tolerance band.
items.short: The Monetary Policy Committee is a six-member statutory body under the RBI Act that fixes the policy repo rate needed to achieve India's inflation target.
body: India moved to a flexible inflation targeting framework through the 2016 amendment to the RBI Act. Section 45ZB set up the MPC, which first met in October 2016. Earlier, the Governor alone decided the policy rate after consulting a technical advisory committee.

The MPC has six members: the RBI Governor (chairperson), a Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer nominated by the central board, and three external members appointed by the Central Government for four years, who cannot be reappointed. The quorum is four, including the Governor or, in his absence, the Deputy Governor. Each member has one vote, decisions are by majority, and the Governor has a casting vote in a tie. It must meet at least four times a year; in practice it meets six times.

The Central Government, in consultation with RBI, sets the target once every five years: 4% CPI inflation with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%. If average inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, it counts as a failure, and RBI must send a report to the government explaining the reasons, remedial actions and expected time to return to target.

After each meeting the MPC publishes a resolution, and minutes appear on the 14th day. The MPC decides only the policy rate and stance (such as neutral or accommodative); CRR, SLR and other operational tools are set by RBI.
items.example: Suppose at an MPC meeting three members vote to cut repo by 25 basis points and three vote to hold. The tie is broken by the Governor's casting vote; if the Governor was among those voting to cut, the repo rate falls, say from 5.50% to 5.25%. SDF moves to 5.00% and MSF and bank rate to 5.50% automatically. If CPI inflation averaged 6.4%, 6.7% and 6.2% in three straight quarters, RBI would have to report its failure to the government.
faqs: Does the Finance Ministry have a vote in the MPC?

No. The government appoints the three external members and sets the inflation target, but no government official sits on or votes in the MPC. Earlier proposals for a government representative were dropped to protect the committee's independence. The government can, however, convey its views in writing.
Which inflation measure does the MPC target?

Headline CPI (combined) inflation published by the National Statistics Office, covering rural and urban India. It does not target WPI or core inflation, although members study core inflation, food prices and expectations surveys when deciding the rate.

items.title: Open Market Operations (OMO): How RBI Manages Liquidity
items.description: OMO means RBI buying or selling government securities in the market to add or remove durable liquidity. Learn OMO purchase vs sale with a worked example.
items.short: Open market operations are outright purchases or sales of government securities by RBI in the market, used to inject or absorb durable liquidity in the banking system.
body: When RBI buys government securities from banks and other market participants (an OMO purchase), it pays them money, which increases bank reserves and liquidity. When RBI sells securities (an OMO sale), buyers pay RBI, and money leaves the system. Unlike repo, these are outright transactions with no promise to reverse, so the effect on liquidity is durable.

RBI conducts OMOs through auctions on its E-Kuber platform or by trading on the NDS-OM screen. OMOs also affect bond yields. An OMO purchase raises demand for bonds, pushing prices up and yields down; a sale does the opposite. In a 'twist' operation, RBI buys long-term and sells short-term securities together, aiming to lower long-term yields without changing total liquidity.

RBI uses OMOs to offset durable liquidity shifts. For example, when RBI buys foreign currency to stop the rupee from rising, it releases rupees; it may then sell bonds through OMOs to absorb the excess, a process called sterilisation. During a deficit, as in heavy forex sales by RBI, OMO purchases add rupees back.

Exam trap: an OMO purchase is expansionary (adds money), an OMO sale is contractionary. Also, OMO is a quantitative tool of monetary policy, along with CRR, SLR and LAF, whereas moral suasion and margin requirements are qualitative tools.
items.example: RBI announces an OMO purchase auction of ₹20,000 crore. A bank sells a 10-year bond with face value ₹1,000 crore at a price of ₹102 per ₹100, so it receives ₹1,020 crore in its RBI current account. Across all sellers, ₹20,000 crore of fresh reserves enters the system. If banks keep 3% as CRR on new deposits created later, the rest can support further lending.
faqs: Is OMO the same as repo?

No. Repo is a temporary loan against securities that is reversed after a fixed period, so liquidity returns to RBI. OMO is an outright sale or purchase, so the change in liquidity is permanent until RBI reverses it with another trade. RBI uses repo for short-term needs and OMO for lasting shifts.
What is sterilisation in OMO?

When RBI buys dollars to manage the exchange rate, it injects rupees into the system. To prevent this from adding to inflation, RBI may sell government securities through OMOs to absorb the same amount of rupees. This offsetting operation is called sterilisation.

items.title: What is Inflation? Meaning, Types and Causes in India
items.description: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level that reduces purchasing power. Learn demand-pull vs cost-push, headline vs core, with examples.
items.short: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general level of prices of goods and services over time, which means each rupee buys less than before.
body: Inflation is measured as the percentage change in a price index over a period, usually year-on-year. In India the main measures are the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which tracks what households pay, and the Wholesale Price Index (WPI), which tracks bulk prices. RBI's Monetary Policy Committee targets CPI inflation of 4% within a 2% to 6% band.

Economists separate causes into two types. Demand-pull inflation happens when spending grows faster than the economy can produce, for example after a big rise in incomes or easy credit. Cost-push inflation comes from higher input costs, such as crude oil, wages or a poor monsoon raising food prices. In India, food and fuel shocks are frequent drivers, which is why policymakers also watch core inflation, which excludes food and fuel and reflects underlying demand pressure.

Inflation hurts people on fixed incomes and savers whose deposit interest does not keep pace. The real interest rate is roughly the nominal rate minus inflation. It can help borrowers, since loans are repaid in cheaper rupees. Moderate, stable inflation is considered healthy; very high or volatile inflation distorts decisions.

Related terms often confused: disinflation means inflation is falling but still positive (prices rise more slowly); deflation means prices actually fall; stagflation is high inflation with weak growth; and the base effect is when a low or high figure in the previous year makes this year's rate look unusually high or low.
items.example: A thali cost ₹100 last year and ₹106 this year, so its price inflation is (106 − 100)/100 = 6%. If your fixed deposit earned 7%, your ₹10,000 grew to ₹10,700, but you now need ₹10,600 to buy what ₹10,000 bought before. Your real gain is only about ₹100, roughly 0.94% (1.07/1.06 − 1). At 8% inflation, the same deposit would lose purchasing power.
faqs: What is the difference between headline and core inflation?

Headline inflation is the change in the full CPI basket, including food and fuel. Core inflation removes these volatile items to show the underlying trend driven by demand. If headline inflation jumps because of a vegetable price spike while core stays steady, the pressure may be temporary and supply-driven.
Is deflation good because things become cheaper?

Not usually. Persistent deflation makes people delay purchases, expecting lower prices, which reduces demand, profits and jobs. It also raises the real burden of debt. Central banks generally prefer low positive inflation to deflation, which is why India's target is 4% rather than zero.

items.title: Consumer Price Index (CPI) India: Meaning and Calculation
items.description: CPI measures change in retail prices paid by households and is RBI's inflation target. Learn who publishes CPI, its types, weights and a worked example.
items.short: The Consumer Price Index measures the change over time in retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by households, and is India's main inflation gauge.
body: The all-India CPI (Rural, Urban and Combined) is compiled by the National Statistics Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) and released monthly, around the 12th. Older series still exist for specific groups: CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) by the Labour Bureau, used for dearness allowance, and CPI for Agricultural and Rural Labourers (CPI-AL and CPI-RL).

The index compares the cost of a basket to its cost in a base year, which is set to 100. Items carry weights based on household consumption surveys. In the 2012-base series, food and beverages had the largest weight, close to half of the combined index, which is why vegetable and pulse prices move CPI so sharply. MoSPI has been revising the base year and weights using newer consumption survey data; check MoSPI for the current base and weights (as of 2026).

CPI Combined inflation is the official target for monetary policy since 2016. Unlike WPI, CPI includes services such as housing, education, health and transport, and uses retail prices, including taxes. That makes it closer to what people actually feel.

A frequent exam mix-up: CPI-IW is published by the Labour Bureau (Ministry of Labour), while CPI Combined is published by NSO. Another: CPI inflation is the year-on-year change in the index, not the index value itself.
items.example: Suppose the CPI Combined index was 192.0 in October last year and 202.8 in October this year. Year-on-year inflation = (202.8 − 192.0)/192.0 × 100 = 5.625%, reported as 5.6%. If the index rose from 201.5 in September to 202.8 in October, the month-on-month change is about 0.65%, which is a different number and should not be confused with annual inflation.
faqs: Why does RBI target CPI and not WPI?

CPI reflects the prices consumers actually pay, including services, so it better captures the cost of living and inflation expectations. WPI covers only goods at the wholesale stage and is heavily influenced by global commodity prices. The Urjit Patel committee in 2014 recommended CPI Combined as the nominal anchor, and the 2016 framework adopted it.
What is CPI-IW used for?

CPI for Industrial Workers, compiled by the Labour Bureau, is used to revise dearness allowance for central government employees and pensioners and for wage indexation in many industries and some public sector banks. It is not the measure used by RBI for its inflation target.

items.title: Wholesale Price Index (WPI): Meaning, Groups, Example
items.description: WPI tracks prices of goods at the wholesale level in India. See who publishes it, its three major groups, how it differs from CPI and a worked example.
items.short: The Wholesale Price Index measures the average change in prices of goods traded in bulk, at the first point of sale, before retail margins and most taxes are added.
body: WPI is compiled and released monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser in the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry, usually around the 14th. The current series uses 2011-12 as base; a revision has been under discussion, so check for a newer series (as of 2026).

The basket is divided into three major groups: Primary Articles (food grains, vegetables, minerals, crude petroleum), Fuel and Power (petrol, diesel, electricity, LPG), and Manufactured Products (textiles, chemicals, metals, food products and more). Manufactured products carry the largest weight, around two-thirds of the index. WPI does not cover services at all.

Until 2014 WPI was India's headline inflation number. Its importance for policy fell when RBI moved to CPI-based targeting, but WPI still matters. It signals input-cost pressure on producers, is used to deflate parts of GDP to arrive at real values, and appears in price escalation clauses in contracts. Since 2017 WPI excludes indirect taxes, aligning it with the GST framework.

Students often think WPI and CPI should move together. They can diverge sharply: when crude oil and metal prices crash globally, WPI can turn negative while CPI stays positive due to food and services. The gap itself is studied as a sign of margin pressure on producers.
items.example: Say the WPI All Commodities index was 150.0 in August last year and 153.3 in August this year. WPI inflation = (153.3 − 150.0)/150.0 × 100 = 2.2%. In the same month CPI inflation might be 5.5% because vegetable prices, rents and school fees rose, none of which (except vegetables) feature in WPI. The 3.3 percentage-point gap shows retail prices running ahead of wholesale prices.
faqs: Why does WPI not include services?

WPI is designed to track prices of goods at the point of bulk transaction, and services are not traded in wholesale markets in the same way. Proposals exist for a separate Producer Price Index (PPI) that would include services and measure prices at each production stage, but WPI itself remains goods-only.
Can WPI inflation be negative while CPI is positive?

Yes. India saw negative WPI inflation in parts of 2015, 2020 and 2023, mostly because of falling global commodity and fuel prices. CPI stayed positive because food, housing and services prices kept rising. Negative WPI is sometimes loosely called wholesale deflation.

items.title: What is GDP? Meaning, Calculation Methods and Example
items.description: GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced within India in a year. Learn nominal vs real GDP, three methods, GDP deflator and an example.
items.short: Gross Domestic Product is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a given period, usually a quarter or a financial year.
body: GDP counts what is produced inside India, whether by Indian or foreign-owned firms. It counts only final goods to avoid double counting: the value of wheat is included through the bread, not separately. In India the National Statistics Office (MoSPI) publishes quarterly and annual estimates, with advance estimates in January and February and revisions later.

There are three ways to calculate it, which should give the same answer. The production method adds value added by all sectors. The expenditure method adds private consumption (C), investment (I), government spending (G) and net exports (X − M). The income method adds wages, rent, interest and profits. India's headline growth figure is real GDP at constant prices, based on the expenditure side, while sector growth is shown through GVA.

Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP removes the effect of price changes by valuing output at base-year prices. The ratio of nominal to real GDP is the GDP deflator, a broad inflation measure. India's long-used base year is 2011-12, and MoSPI has been moving to a newer base year; check MoSPI for the current series (as of 2026).

Related measures: GNP (or GNI) adds net income Indians earn from abroad; NDP subtracts depreciation. GDP per capita divides GDP by population. Common confusion: GDP measures output, not welfare, inequality or environmental damage.
items.example: Suppose nominal GDP rises from ₹300 lakh crore to ₹330 lakh crore, a 10% nominal increase. If the GDP deflator rose 3.5%, real growth ≈ 1.10/1.035 − 1 = 6.28%. In the expenditure method, if C = ₹180, I = ₹100, G = ₹35 and net exports = ₹15 lakh crore (X − M), GDP = 180 + 100 + 35 + 15 = ₹330 lakh crore.
faqs: What is the difference between GDP and GNP?

GDP measures production within India's borders regardless of who owns the factors of production. GNP, now usually called GNI, adds income earned by Indian residents abroad and subtracts income earned by foreigners in India. For India, GNI is slightly lower than GDP because net factor income from abroad is negative.
Why are GDP figures revised so often?

Early estimates rely on partial data and indicators like tax collections and industrial output. As fuller data from company filings, surveys and states arrive, NSO publishes first, second and third revised estimates. A base-year revision can also change past numbers. So the first quarterly figure is a provisional reading, not the final word.

items.title: Gross Value Added (GVA) Meaning and Link to GDP
items.description: GVA measures value added by each sector of the economy. Learn the GVA formula, how GVA becomes GDP through taxes and subsidies, and a solved example.
items.short: Gross Value Added is the value of output of a sector or the whole economy minus the value of intermediate goods and services used up in producing it.
body: GVA looks at the economy from the producer's side. For each firm, GVA = value of output − intermediate consumption. A bakery that sells bread worth ₹10 lakh and spends ₹6 lakh on flour, fuel and packaging adds ₹4 lakh of value. Adding this across all producers gives the economy's GVA.

India reports GVA at basic prices, which includes production taxes and excludes production subsidies, but not product taxes like GST. The link is: GDP at market prices = GVA at basic prices + product taxes − product subsidies. So if tax collections rise sharply, GDP can grow faster than GVA, and when subsidies jump, GDP growth can lag GVA.

GVA is split by sector: agriculture, forestry and fishing; industry (mining, manufacturing, electricity, construction); and services (trade, hotels, transport, financial, real estate, public administration and others). This makes it the preferred measure to see which parts of the economy are driving or dragging growth. Services account for more than half of India's GVA.

Exam questions often ask for the formula or why GVA and GDP growth differ. Remember that GVA tells you about supply, while GDP's expenditure side tells you about demand. India adopted GVA reporting with the 2011-12 base revision in 2015, following the UN System of National Accounts.
items.example: Assume GVA at basic prices is ₹270 lakh crore, product taxes (GST, customs, excise) are ₹32 lakh crore and product subsidies (food, fertiliser, fuel) are ₹6 lakh crore. GDP = 270 + 32 − 6 = ₹296 lakh crore. If next year GVA rises 6% to ₹286.2 lakh crore, taxes rise 12% to ₹35.84 lakh crore and subsidies stay at ₹6 lakh crore, GDP becomes ₹316.04 lakh crore, about 6.8% growth, faster than GVA.
faqs: Why does India report both GDP and GVA growth?

GVA shows sector-wise production and avoids distortions from changes in tax rates or subsidies, so it is better for judging economic activity. GDP is the internationally standard headline figure used for comparisons and for ratios like fiscal deficit to GDP. Reporting both gives a fuller picture.
What is the difference between GVA at basic prices and at factor cost?

GVA at factor cost excludes all taxes and includes all subsidies. GVA at basic prices adds production taxes (like land revenue or stamp duty) and subtracts production subsidies, but still excludes product taxes. India switched from factor cost to basic prices in the 2015 revision.

items.title: Fiscal Deficit Meaning, Formula and Example (India)
items.description: Fiscal deficit is the gap between government spending and receipts other than borrowing. Learn the formula, FRBM Act, how it's financed, with an example.
items.short: Fiscal deficit is the amount by which the government's total expenditure exceeds its total receipts excluding borrowings, showing how much it must borrow in a year.
body: Formula: Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − (Revenue receipts + Non-debt capital receipts). Revenue receipts are tax and non-tax revenue. Non-debt capital receipts include disinvestment proceeds and recovery of loans. Borrowings are excluded because the deficit measures exactly how much needs to be borrowed. It is usually stated as a percentage of GDP.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 set targets to reduce the deficit, later amended to add a debt-to-GDP anchor. The Union Budget announces a target each year; for 2025-26 it was 4.4% of GDP, and the government has signalled a shift toward focusing on reducing debt as a share of GDP. Check the latest Union Budget for current targets (as of 2026). States have their own limits, broadly around 3% of state GDP with conditional relaxations.

Why it matters: a high fiscal deficit means more government borrowing, which can push up interest rates and crowd out private borrowers, add to inflation if financed by money creation, and increase future interest burdens. But deficits used for capital spending on roads, railways and power can raise long-term growth, so economists look at its quality as well as its size.

It is financed mainly through market borrowings (dated securities and treasury bills), small savings (via the NSSF) and external loans. Since 1997, direct monetisation through ad hoc treasury bills by RBI has ended.
items.example: Suppose the Centre's total expenditure is ₹50 lakh crore, revenue receipts are ₹34 lakh crore, and non-debt capital receipts (disinvestment plus loan recoveries) are ₹0.8 lakh crore. Fiscal deficit = 50 − (34 + 0.8) = ₹15.2 lakh crore. If GDP is ₹350 lakh crore, the deficit is 15.2/350 = 4.34% of GDP. If interest payments are ₹12.5 lakh crore, the primary deficit is ₹2.7 lakh crore.
faqs: Is a fiscal deficit always bad?

No. Governments often run deficits to fund infrastructure or support the economy in a slowdown, as India did during 2020-21. The concern is sustained high deficits used for consumption spending, which raise debt without boosting future growth. That is why the revenue deficit and the share of capital expenditure are watched closely.
What is the difference between fiscal deficit and budget deficit?

Budget deficit is an older, narrower term, roughly total expenditure minus total receipts including some borrowing like treasury bills. India stopped using it officially in 1997-98 and now reports fiscal, revenue, effective revenue and primary deficits. In most exams, fiscal deficit is the key measure.

items.title: Revenue Deficit Meaning, Formula and Effective RD
items.description: Revenue deficit is the excess of government revenue expenditure over revenue receipts. Learn the formula, effective revenue deficit and why it is a worry.
items.short: Revenue deficit is the excess of the government's revenue expenditure over its revenue receipts, showing that it is borrowing to meet day-to-day running costs.
body: Revenue receipts are tax revenue (income tax, corporation tax, GST, customs, excise, net of states' share) and non-tax revenue (dividends from RBI and PSUs, fees, interest received). Revenue expenditure covers spending that creates no asset: salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies and grants. Formula: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts.

A revenue deficit is considered worse than a fiscal deficit of the same size because the borrowed money is used for consumption rather than investment. It adds to debt without creating assets that could generate future income. That is why the FRBM framework originally aimed to eliminate the revenue deficit altogether.

Effective revenue deficit (ERD) refines this. A large part of the Centre's revenue expenditure is grants to states for creating capital assets, such as roads under centrally sponsored schemes. These are revenue spending in the Centre's books but build assets in the economy. ERD = Revenue deficit − Grants for creation of capital assets. The concept was introduced in the 2011-12 Budget.

Exam pointers: interest payments are revenue expenditure, so they push up the revenue deficit; loans given by the government to states or PSUs are capital expenditure, not revenue. Disinvestment proceeds are capital receipts and do not reduce the revenue deficit. India's revenue deficit has been positive for most years since the 1980s.
items.example: Suppose revenue receipts are ₹34 lakh crore and revenue expenditure is ₹39 lakh crore. Revenue deficit = 39 − 34 = ₹5 lakh crore. If ₹3.2 lakh crore of that spending is grants to states for creating capital assets, the effective revenue deficit = 5 − 3.2 = ₹1.8 lakh crore. With a fiscal deficit of ₹15.2 lakh crore, about 5/15.2 = 33% of borrowing finances revenue spending.
faqs: Are interest payments revenue or capital expenditure?

Interest payments are revenue expenditure because they do not create any asset; they are a cost of past borrowing. They are the single largest item of the Centre's revenue spending. Repayment of the principal of a loan, by contrast, is a capital expenditure item.
Can disinvestment reduce the revenue deficit?

No. Selling government shares in PSUs brings non-debt capital receipts, which reduce the fiscal deficit but not the revenue deficit. Using one-time asset sales to fund recurring spending is criticised because the government loses the asset while the spending continues next year.

items.title: Primary Deficit Meaning: Formula and Why It Matters
items.description: Primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest payments. Learn what it reveals about current fiscal policy, debt sustainability and a quick example.
items.short: Primary deficit is the fiscal deficit minus interest payments on past borrowing, showing how much the government is borrowing for its current-year spending alone.
body: Formula: Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments. The fiscal deficit includes interest on debt taken in earlier years, which the present government cannot avoid. Removing it isolates the gap caused by this year's policy choices on spending and taxes.

If the primary deficit is zero, the government is borrowing only to pay interest on old debt. A primary surplus means current revenues more than cover non-interest spending, and some of the interest is also being paid from revenue. Countries trying to bring down debt often aim for a primary surplus.

Primary deficit is central to debt sustainability. The debt-to-GDP ratio stays stable or falls when the primary balance is close to zero and nominal GDP growth exceeds the interest rate on debt. India's high interest burden, which takes up a large share of the Centre's revenue receipts, means that even a modest primary deficit can keep debt high.

Common confusion: some students subtract interest receipts too. The standard definition subtracts only interest payments. Also, primary deficit is not the same as revenue deficit; the latter compares revenue expenditure with revenue receipts and ignores capital spending.
items.example: Take a fiscal deficit of ₹15.7 lakh crore and interest payments of ₹12.8 lakh crore. Primary deficit = 15.7 − 12.8 = ₹2.9 lakh crore. With GDP of ₹357 lakh crore, it is 2.9/357 = 0.81% of GDP. If next year interest payments rise to ₹13.6 lakh crore while the fiscal deficit stays at ₹15.7 lakh crore, the primary deficit falls to ₹2.1 lakh crore, meaning current policy got tighter even though the headline deficit didn't change.
faqs: What does a primary surplus mean?

A primary surplus means revenue and non-debt receipts exceed all spending except interest payments. The government is then using part of its own income to service old debt rather than borrowing for it. Sustained primary surpluses are one way countries reduce their debt-to-GDP ratio.
Why is primary deficit called a measure of current fiscal stance?

Interest payments depend on past borrowing and past interest rates, which the current government cannot change. By removing them, primary deficit shows whether today's decisions on taxes and spending are expansionary or contractionary, making it a cleaner indicator of present policy.

items.title: Current Account Deficit (CAD) Meaning with Example
items.description: CAD is the excess of India's payments to the world over receipts for goods, services, income and transfers. Learn components, financing and a worked case.
items.short: Current account deficit arises when a country's payments to the rest of the world for goods, services, income and transfers exceed what it receives from abroad in a period.
body: The current account is one half of the balance of payments (BoP); the other is the capital and financial account. The current account has four parts: merchandise trade (goods exports minus imports), services trade (IT, travel, transport), primary income (interest, dividends, wages earned or paid abroad) and secondary income (mostly remittances). Services, primary income and transfers together are called invisibles.

India runs a large merchandise trade deficit because of crude oil, gold and electronics imports. This is offset partly by a services surplus led by software exports and by large remittances from Indians abroad. The net result is usually a modest CAD, commonly between about 1% and 3% of GDP. RBI publishes quarterly BoP data.

A CAD must be financed by capital inflows: foreign direct investment, foreign portfolio investment, external commercial borrowings or NRI deposits. If inflows fall short, RBI draws down forex reserves. A widening CAD with weak inflows puts pressure on the rupee, as in 2013, when India was grouped with the 'Fragile Five' economies.

Watch the twin deficits idea: a high fiscal deficit can widen the CAD because government borrowing raises demand, including for imports. Also note that a current account surplus is not automatically good; India had one in 2020-21 mainly because imports collapsed during the pandemic.
items.example: In a quarter, suppose goods exports are $110 billion and imports $175 billion, a trade deficit of $65 billion. Net services bring in $45 billion, net remittances $30 billion, and net primary income is −$12 billion. CAD = −65 + 45 + 30 − 12 = −$2 billion, a small deficit. If quarterly GDP is $1,000 billion, that is 0.2% of GDP. A $15 billion jump in oil imports would raise it to $17 billion, or 1.7%.
faqs: What is the difference between CAD and trade deficit?

Trade deficit usually refers only to goods: merchandise imports minus exports. CAD is broader and also includes services, income flows and transfers like remittances. India's trade deficit is much larger than its CAD because services exports and remittances cover a big part of the goods gap.
How does a high CAD affect the rupee?

A CAD means more foreign currency is needed for payments than earned. If capital inflows do not fill the gap, demand for dollars exceeds supply and the rupee weakens. RBI may sell dollars from reserves to smooth the fall, but a persistent large CAD is a source of currency vulnerability.

items.title: Fiscal Policy Meaning: Tools, Types and vs Monetary Policy
items.description: Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxes, spending and borrowing to steer the economy. Learn expansionary vs contractionary tools and key differences.
items.short: Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxation, public expenditure and borrowing to influence demand, growth, employment, prices and income distribution in the economy.
body: In India, the Union Government sets fiscal policy through the annual Union Budget presented by the Finance Minister under Article 112 of the Constitution, and state governments do the same through state budgets. Its tools are tax rates and structure (income tax, GST, customs), public spending (on infrastructure, subsidies, welfare schemes) and the size and form of borrowing.

Expansionary fiscal policy means cutting taxes or raising spending to boost demand, usually during a slowdown. It widens the fiscal deficit. Contractionary policy, raising taxes or cutting spending, cools an overheated economy and reduces the deficit. Automatic stabilisers, such as tax collections that fall in a recession, work even without new decisions.

Fiscal policy differs from monetary policy in who runs it and how it acts. Monetary policy is run by RBI through interest rates and liquidity and works broadly across the economy. Fiscal policy is run by the government and can target specific sectors, regions or groups, such as a capital expenditure push or a fertiliser subsidy. The two should ideally complement each other; a very loose fiscal policy can force RBI to keep rates higher to control inflation.

Fiscal discipline in India is guided by the FRBM Act, 2003. The multiplier effect explains why ₹1 of public spending can raise GDP by more than ₹1: the money becomes someone's income and is spent again.
items.example: Suppose the government spends an extra ₹1 lakh crore on highways, and households spend 75% of any extra income (marginal propensity to consume 0.75). The simple multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4, so total demand could rise by up to ₹4 lakh crore. In reality leakages such as taxes and imports lower the multiplier, so studies for India often find capital spending multipliers well below this textbook figure, though higher than for revenue spending.
faqs: Who controls fiscal policy in India?

The Union Government through the Ministry of Finance controls central fiscal policy, approved by Parliament through the Budget and Finance Bill. State governments run their own fiscal policies through state legislatures. The GST Council, with both Centre and states, decides GST rates. RBI has no role in setting fiscal policy.
What is crowding out?

When the government borrows heavily, it competes with private firms for the same pool of savings. This can push up interest rates and reduce private investment. The effect is called crowding out and is one argument for keeping fiscal deficits under control, especially when the economy is already near full capacity.

items.title: Money Supply M0, M1, M3 Meaning: Narrow vs Broad Money
items.description: Money supply measures the stock of money in the economy. Learn RBI's M0, M1, M2 and M3, what each includes, the money multiplier and a worked example.
items.short: Money supply is the total stock of money available in an economy at a point of time, measured by RBI through aggregates such as M0, M1 and M3.
body: RBI publishes money aggregates fortnightly. Reserve money (M0), also called base money or high-powered money, is currency in circulation plus bankers' deposits with RBI plus other deposits with RBI. It is the money RBI directly creates.

M1 (narrow money) = currency with the public + demand deposits with banks (current accounts and the demand portion of savings accounts) + other deposits with RBI. M2 adds savings deposits with post office savings banks. M3 (broad money) = M1 + time deposits with banks (fixed and recurring deposits). M4 adds total post office deposits. M3 is the most watched measure of money growth in India. RBI also compiles new liquidity aggregates (L1, L2, L3) suggested by a 1998 working group.

The money multiplier links them: M3 = m × M0. When banks receive deposits, they keep a fraction as reserves (CRR) and lend the rest, which is redeposited and lent again. A lower CRR or more lending raises the multiplier. That is why RBI's actions on reserve money can expand broad money several times.

Common exam trap: liquidity decreases as you move from M1 to M4 because time deposits are less readily spendable than cash. Also, 'other deposits with RBI' are deposits of quasi-government bodies, foreign central banks and similar entities, not of commercial banks.
items.example: Suppose currency with the public is ₹35 lakh crore, demand deposits ₹30 lakh crore, other deposits with RBI ₹1 lakh crore, and bank time deposits ₹200 lakh crore. M1 = 35 + 30 + 1 = ₹66 lakh crore; M3 = 66 + 200 = ₹266 lakh crore. If reserve money is ₹48 lakh crore, the money multiplier = 266/48 = about 5.5.
faqs: Which measure of money supply is called broad money?

M3 is called broad money. It includes currency with the public, demand deposits, other deposits with RBI and time deposits with banks. M1 is called narrow money. RBI gives most attention to M3 when analysing growth of money and its link with inflation and credit.
Why is M0 called high-powered money?

M0 is the base on which banks create deposits through lending. Every rupee of reserve money can support several rupees of broad money through the multiplier process, so changes in M0 have a magnified effect on the overall money supply. Only RBI can create M0.

items.title: What is Stagflation? Meaning, Causes and Policy Dilemma
items.description: Stagflation combines high inflation with slow growth and rising unemployment. Learn its causes, why it is hard for RBI to fix and global and Indian examples.
items.short: Stagflation is a situation where an economy suffers high inflation, weak or stagnant growth and rising unemployment at the same time.
body: The word combines 'stagnation' and 'inflation'. Traditional thinking, illustrated by the Phillips curve, held that inflation and unemployment move in opposite directions: when the economy is booming, prices rise but jobs are plentiful. Stagflation breaks that pattern, which is why it surprised economists in the 1970s.

The classic cause is a supply shock. When oil prices quadrupled after 1973 and rose again in 1979, costs rose for almost every business. Firms raised prices and cut output, so inflation rose while growth fell. Other causes include poor harvests, wage-price spirals where workers demand higher pay and firms pass it on, and policy mistakes such as printing money while growth is weak.

Stagflation is a policy dilemma. If the central bank raises rates to fight inflation, growth weakens further. If it cuts rates to support growth, inflation can rise. Governments face similar trade-offs with spending. Usually the solution involves fixing the supply problem, anchoring inflation expectations, and accepting some short-term pain.

India faced stagflation-like conditions in the early 1970s and around 2011-13, when CPI inflation stayed near double digits while GDP growth slowed. Exam questions often ask which curve it contradicts (Phillips curve), what type of inflation is usually behind it (cost-push) and the main policy challenge.
items.example: Suppose an economy grew 7% with 5% inflation last year. A crude oil shock lifts fuel costs 40%, transport and fertiliser costs follow, and inflation jumps to 8%. Factories cut shifts, so growth slows to 4% and unemployment rises from 7% to 8.5%. If the central bank raises its policy rate from 6% to 7% to tame prices, businesses face costlier loans and growth may slip further, showing the stagflation dilemma.
faqs: What is the difference between stagflation and recession?

A recession is a significant decline in economic activity, often defined as two consecutive quarters of falling GDP, and usually comes with low or falling inflation. Stagflation combines weak growth, which may or may not be negative, with high inflation. The added inflation makes stagflation harder to treat with ordinary rate cuts.
What type of inflation causes stagflation?

Stagflation is usually driven by cost-push inflation, where higher input costs such as oil, food or wages push prices up and reduce output at the same time. Demand-pull inflation, by contrast, comes with strong growth, so it rarely produces stagflation on its own.

items.title: What is NPA? Non-Performing Asset Meaning with Example
items.description: An NPA is a loan whose interest or principal is overdue for more than 90 days. Learn gross vs net NPA, how banks classify NPAs and a worked example.
items.short: A non-performing asset is a loan or advance on which interest or principal instalment remains overdue for more than 90 days, so it stops generating income for the bank.
body: Under RBI's prudential norms, a term loan becomes an NPA if interest or instalment is overdue for more than 90 days. A cash credit or overdraft account becomes NPA if it remains 'out of order' for more than 90 days, meaning the balance stays above the sanctioned limit or drawing power, or no credits come in enough to cover interest. Bills purchased and discounted become NPA if overdue for more than 90 days. For agricultural loans, the period is linked to crop seasons: two crop seasons for short-duration crops and one for long-duration crops.

Once an account is an NPA, the bank cannot book interest as income until it is actually received, and it must set aside provisions from profits. Classification is done borrower-wise, not facility-wise: if one loan of a borrower is NPA, all facilities to that borrower with the same bank become NPA.

Gross NPA is the total of all NPA loans. Net NPA = Gross NPA − Provisions held. Both are expressed as a percentage of total advances. Rising NPAs hurt bank profits, capital and lending capacity, which is why the 2015 Asset Quality Review and later recovery laws like the IBC were major events in Indian banking.

A common misunderstanding is that a loan becomes NPA on the 90th day. It becomes NPA when overdue for more than 90 days, so the 91st day of continuous overdue status. Also, NPA status is now updated daily as part of the day-end process, not just at the quarter-end.
items.example: An EMI of ₹25,000 on a business loan was due on 1 April and remains unpaid. On 30 June it has been overdue for 90 days; on 1 July it becomes 91 days overdue and the account turns NPA. If the bank's gross advances are ₹1,00,000 crore, gross NPAs ₹4,000 crore and provisions ₹2,800 crore, gross NPA ratio = 4%, net NPA = ₹1,200 crore, about 1.25% of net advances (1,200/97,200).
faqs: What is the difference between gross NPA and net NPA?

Gross NPA is the total outstanding of all loans classified as non-performing. Net NPA deducts the provisions the bank has already made against those loans. Net NPA shows the bank's real exposure to bad loans after cushioning. A bank with high gross NPA but strong provisions may have low net NPA.
Can an NPA account become standard again?

Yes. If the borrower pays all overdue interest and principal, the account can be upgraded to standard. For restructured accounts, upgrade happens only after satisfactory performance during a specified period. Partial payments that leave dues overdue beyond 90 days do not upgrade the account.

items.term: IRAC Norms (Income Recognition and Asset Classification)
items.title: IRAC Norms: Asset Classification and Provisioning Rules
items.description: IRAC norms are RBI rules on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning for loans. Learn substandard, doubtful and loss assets with examples.
items.short: IRAC norms are RBI's prudential rules on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and provisioning, which decide when a loan is bad and how much a bank must set aside for it.
body: Introduced in 1992-93 following the Narasimham Committee, IRAC norms brought Indian bank accounting close to international practice. Income recognition: interest on an NPA cannot be booked on accrual basis; it is recognised only when actually received. Interest already booked but not collected is reversed when the account turns NPA.

Asset classification puts loans into four categories. Standard assets are performing loans. Substandard assets have remained NPA for up to 12 months. Doubtful assets have remained in substandard category for 12 months; they are further split into D1 (doubtful up to 1 year), D2 (1 to 3 years) and D3 (more than 3 years). Loss assets are those identified by the bank, auditors or RBI as uncollectible, even if not written off.

Provisioning rises with age. Broad current rates: standard assets generally 0.40% (higher for some sectors, lower for farm and SME loans); substandard 15% (25% if unsecured); doubtful: 100% of the unsecured portion plus, on the secured portion, 25% for D1, 40% for D2 and 100% for D3; loss assets 100%. RBI has proposed shifting to an expected credit loss approach, so check current RBI circulars (as of 2026).

Classic trap: the 12-month clocks run from the date of becoming NPA, not from the date of default. Also, erosion in security value can make RBI treat an account as doubtful or loss directly, without waiting.
items.example: A ₹50 lakh loan with security realisable at ₹30 lakh turned NPA on 1 April 2023. It is substandard till 31 March 2024, needing 15% × 50 = ₹7.5 lakh. From 1 April 2024 it is D1: unsecured ₹20 lakh × 100% + secured ₹30 lakh × 25% = ₹27.5 lakh. In D2 (from April 2025): 20 + 30 × 40% = ₹32 lakh. In D3: the full ₹50 lakh.
faqs: How long does an account remain substandard?

An account remains substandard for a maximum of 12 months from the date it became an NPA. After that, if not upgraded, it moves to doubtful category. If the security is seriously eroded or fraud is involved, it may be downgraded faster, directly to doubtful or loss.
Why is provision higher for unsecured loans?

If a secured loan fails, the bank can sell the security to recover part of the dues. An unsecured loan has no such backstop, so the expected loss is higher. RBI therefore requires extra provisioning on unsecured exposures, such as 25% instead of 15% in substandard and 100% on the unsecured part of doubtful assets.

items.title: Special Mention Account (SMA-0, SMA-1, SMA-2) Explained
items.description: SMA is RBI's early-warning category for loans showing stress before they turn NPA. Learn SMA-0, SMA-1 and SMA-2 day buckets with a worked example.
items.short: A Special Mention Account is a loan that is still standard but shows early signs of stress, classified by how many days payments are overdue before it becomes an NPA.
body: RBI introduced SMA categories in 2014 under its framework for early recognition of financial distress, and refined them in the 2019 Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets. For loans other than revolving facilities, the buckets are: SMA-0 when principal or interest is overdue for 1 to 30 days; SMA-1 for more than 30 and up to 60 days; and SMA-2 for more than 60 and up to 90 days. Beyond 90 days the account becomes an NPA.

For cash credit and overdraft accounts, the SMA-1 and SMA-2 buckets are based on how long the account has been continuously out of order: more than 30 up to 60 days for SMA-1, and more than 60 up to 90 days for SMA-2.

Banks report SMA status of borrowers with aggregate exposure of ₹5 crore and above to RBI's Central Repository of Information on Large Credits (CRILC). Under the 2019 framework, lenders must review a borrower's account within 30 days of default and, for large exposures, may sign an inter-creditor agreement and implement a resolution plan within 180 days, failing which additional provisions apply.

SMA status also matters to borrowers: it is reported to credit bureaus and can affect credit scores. A common error is treating SMA as an NPA category; it is still a standard asset, so interest is booked normally and only the standard-asset provision applies.
items.example: A borrower's EMI due on 5 January is unpaid. On 6 January the account is SMA-0. On 5 February it is still overdue (31 days), so it moves to SMA-1. On 7 March, overdue 61 days, it becomes SMA-2. If nothing is paid and the overdue period reaches 91 days on 6 April, it slips into NPA. Paying the January EMI on 10 February but missing February's EMI keeps the oldest overdue at the February date, so the account stays in SMA.
faqs: Is an SMA account an NPA?

No. An SMA is still a standard asset. The classification is an early warning so lenders can act before the account turns bad. Interest continues to be recognised as income, and only standard-asset provisioning applies, although banks may watch the account more closely or start a resolution process.
Does SMA status affect my credit score?

Yes. Banks report overdue days to credit information companies like CIBIL, and repeated SMA status signals payment stress. Even short delays of a few days show up as days past due. Paying dues before they are overdue is the simplest way to keep the record clean.

items.title: Provision Coverage Ratio (PCR): Formula and Meaning
items.description: PCR shows what share of a bank's bad loans is already covered by provisions. Learn the formula, with and without write-offs, and how to read a bank's PCR.
items.short: Provision coverage ratio is the percentage of a bank's gross non-performing assets that it has already covered by setting aside provisions from its profits.
body: Basic formula: PCR = Total provisions held for NPAs ÷ Gross NPAs × 100. A higher PCR means the bank has already absorbed more of the expected loss in its accounts, so future earnings and capital are better protected. Analysts treat PCR as a measure of balance-sheet conservatism.

Banks often report two versions. PCR excluding technical write-offs uses only provisions against NPAs still on the books. PCR including technical write-offs adds loans that have been fully provided and removed from the balance sheet but are still being pursued for recovery; it adds these amounts to both the provisions and the gross NPA figures, which pushes the ratio higher. When comparing banks, check which version is quoted.

RBI required banks to reach a PCR of 70% by September 2011, a requirement later withdrawn in favour of building countercyclical buffers. There is no standalone mandatory PCR now, but RBI and investors monitor it closely; Indian banks improved PCR significantly after the post-2015 asset quality clean-up.
Link with net NPA: Net NPA = Gross NPA − Provisions. So a high PCR directly lowers net NPA. A bank with a 4% gross NPA ratio and 75% PCR will have net NPA of about 1% of advances.
items.example: A bank has gross NPAs of ₹8,000 crore and specific provisions of ₹6,000 crore. PCR = 6,000/8,000 = 75%. Net NPA = ₹2,000 crore. It has also technically written off ₹4,000 crore (fully provided). Including write-offs, PCR = (6,000 + 4,000)/(8,000 + 4,000) = 10,000/12,000 = 83.3%. The same bank can quote either figure.
faqs: Is a higher PCR always better?

A higher PCR means the bank is better cushioned against bad loans and less likely to face earnings shocks later. However, very high provisioning reduces current profits. Investors generally prefer a high PCR, especially when gross NPAs are elevated, but they also look at recoveries, slippages and capital adequacy.
What is a technical write-off?

A technical write-off removes a fully provided NPA from the bank's balance sheet for accounting purposes, while the bank continues its legal recovery efforts. The borrower's liability is not waived. Any later recovery is booked as income. It differs from a compromise settlement, where the bank actually agrees to accept less.

items.title: Priority Sector Lending (PSL): Targets and Categories
items.description: PSL requires banks to lend a set share of credit to agriculture, MSMEs, weaker sections and others. Learn the 40% ANBC target, sub-targets and PSLCs.
items.short: Priority sector lending is RBI's requirement that banks direct a minimum share of their credit to sectors considered important for development, like agriculture, MSMEs and weaker sections.
body: The idea dates back to 1972, after bank nationalisation, when the government wanted credit to reach farmers and small businesses. Today RBI's Master Directions list eight categories: agriculture, micro small and medium enterprises, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewable energy, and others (including loans to weaker sections and small personal loans to distressed persons).

For domestic scheduled commercial banks and foreign banks with 20 or more branches, the overall target is 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure (CEOBE), whichever is higher. Sub-targets include 18% for agriculture (with a part reserved for small and marginal farmers), 7.5% for micro enterprises, and a share for weaker sections. RRBs and small finance banks have higher overall targets. These percentages have been revised several times, so check the latest RBI Master Direction (as of 2026).

Banks that fall short must deposit the shortfall in funds like the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) with NABARD or similar funds with SIDBI and NHB, at below-market interest rates. Since 2016, banks can also trade Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs) on RBI's e-Kuber platform: a bank with surplus PSL loans sells certificates to a bank with a shortfall, without transferring the loans.
Common mistakes: not every agricultural loan qualifies (limits apply to some categories), and housing loans qualify only up to set amount limits based on city population.
items.example: A bank's ANBC is ₹2,00,000 crore. PSL target = 40% = ₹80,000 crore; agriculture sub-target = 18% = ₹36,000 crore; micro enterprises = 7.5% = ₹15,000 crore. If the bank's agri lending is only ₹33,000 crore, it has a ₹3,000 crore shortfall. It can buy agriculture PSLCs worth ₹3,000 crore from a bank with surplus, paying a fee set in the auction, say 1.2%, which is ₹36 crore.
faqs: What is ANBC in priority sector lending?

Adjusted Net Bank Credit is broadly the bank's net bank credit plus certain investments in non-SLR bonds held to maturity, minus specified exclusions like certain refinance and eligible bills rediscounted. PSL targets are calculated on the higher of ANBC or the credit equivalent of off-balance sheet exposures, as of the corresponding date of the previous year.
Do PSLCs transfer the actual loans?

No. Priority Sector Lending Certificates transfer only the PSL credit, not the loans or their credit risk. The selling bank keeps the loans on its books, while the buying bank can count the certificate towards its target. Certificates are traded on RBI's e-Kuber platform and expire at the end of the financial year.

items.title: Basel III Norms in India: Pillars, Capital, Buffers
items.description: Basel III is the global framework for bank capital and liquidity. Learn its three pillars, India's capital ratios, buffers, leverage ratio and LCR rules.
items.short: Basel III is a set of international banking standards from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision that requires banks to hold more and better-quality capital and liquidity to absorb losses.
body: The Basel Committee, hosted by the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, Switzerland, issued Basel I (1988) on credit risk capital, Basel II (2004) with three pillars, and Basel III (2010) after the global financial crisis exposed thin capital and weak liquidity. India began implementing Basel III in April 2013 in phases.

The three pillars are: Pillar 1, minimum capital requirements for credit, market and operational risk; Pillar 2, supervisory review, where banks assess their overall risks (ICAAP) and supervisors can require more capital; and Pillar 3, market discipline through public disclosures.

India's Basel III requirements are stricter than the global minimum. Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) of 5.5% of risk-weighted assets, Tier 1 capital of 7%, and total capital (CRAR) of 9%, plus a Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB) of 2.5% in CET1, making 11.5% overall. Domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs) like SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank carry an extra CET1 surcharge. A countercyclical buffer can be activated in boom times. These figures are as of 2026; check RBI's Master Circular.

Basel III also added liquidity standards, the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), both at 100%, and a leverage ratio (4% for D-SIBs and 3.5% for other banks in India) to cap borrowing irrespective of risk weights.
items.example: A bank has risk-weighted assets of ₹1,00,000 crore. It needs CET1 of 5.5% + 2.5% CCB = ₹8,000 crore, Tier 1 of 7% + 2.5% = ₹9,500 crore, and total capital of 11.5% = ₹11,500 crore. If it holds CET1 of ₹9,000 crore, AT1 bonds of ₹1,000 crore and Tier 2 of ₹2,500 crore, total capital is ₹12,500 crore, or 12.5%, comfortably above the minimum.
faqs: Why are India's Basel III norms stricter than global ones?

RBI set total capital at 9% against the Basel minimum of 8%, and CET1 at 5.5% against 4.5%. The higher bar reflects RBI's conservative approach given India's history of bad loans and the importance of public confidence in banks. Extra buffers on top provide further protection.
What is the Capital Conservation Buffer?
