It is an extra 2.5% of risk-weighted assets that banks must hold in common equity above the minimum. In good times it builds a cushion. If a bank dips into the buffer, it faces restrictions on dividends and bonus payouts until it rebuilds capital, which conserves capital during stress.

items.title: Capital Adequacy Ratio (CRAR): Formula and Example
items.description: CRAR measures a bank's capital against its risk-weighted assets. Learn the formula, Tier 1 vs Tier 2 capital, risk weights and India's minimum requirement.
items.short: Capital adequacy ratio, or capital to risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR), is a bank's capital expressed as a percentage of its risk-weighted assets, showing its ability to absorb losses.
body: Formula: CRAR = (Tier 1 capital + Tier 2 capital) ÷ Risk-weighted assets × 100. Tier 1 is core capital: equity share capital, reserves and retained profits (Common Equity Tier 1), plus Additional Tier 1 instruments such as perpetual bonds. Tier 2 is supplementary capital: certain subordinated debt, general provisions within limits and revaluation reserves at a discount.

Risk-weighted assets (RWA) recognise that not every loan is equally risky. Each asset is multiplied by a risk weight. Cash and central government securities carry 0%; a home loan with a low loan-to-value ratio might carry a lower weight than an unsecured personal loan; a corporate loan's weight depends on its credit rating. RWA also includes charges for market risk and operational risk.

In India, banks must maintain a minimum CRAR of 9% under Basel III, plus a 2.5% capital conservation buffer, effectively 11.5%. Small finance banks and payments banks have a higher minimum of 15%. NBFCs have their own CRAR norms of 15%. These are as of 2026; verify with RBI.

Why it matters: a bank with low CRAR cannot grow its loan book without raising capital, and RBI may place it under Prompt Corrective Action (PCA), which restricts lending, branch expansion and dividends. Investors and depositors watch CRAR as a basic health indicator.
items.example: A bank has: cash and government securities ₹40,000 crore (0% weight), home loans ₹30,000 crore (35% weight), corporate loans ₹50,000 crore (100%), and unsecured retail ₹10,000 crore (125%). Credit RWA = 0 + 10,500 + 50,000 + 12,500 = ₹73,000 crore. Add ₹7,000 crore for market and operational risk: RWA = ₹80,000 crore. With Tier 1 of ₹8,800 crore and Tier 2 of ₹1,600 crore, CRAR = 10,400/80,000 = 13%.
faqs: What is the minimum CRAR for Indian banks?

Scheduled commercial banks must maintain total capital of at least 9% of risk-weighted assets, plus a 2.5% capital conservation buffer in common equity, making 11.5% overall. D-SIBs need an additional surcharge. Small finance banks and payments banks must maintain 15%. These figures are as of 2026; check RBI's latest master circular.
Is CRAR the same as leverage ratio?

No. CRAR divides capital by risk-weighted assets, so risky assets need more capital. The leverage ratio divides Tier 1 capital by total exposure without risk weights, acting as a simple backstop to stop banks from building huge balance sheets of assets with low risk weights.

items.title: Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR): Meaning and Formula
items.description: LCR requires banks to hold enough high-quality liquid assets to survive 30 days of stressed outflows. Learn the formula, HQLA levels and a worked example.
items.short: Liquidity coverage ratio requires a bank to hold enough high-quality liquid assets to cover its expected net cash outflows over a 30-day period of severe stress.
body: LCR is a Basel III liquidity standard. Formula: LCR = Stock of high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) ÷ Total net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar days × 100. The ratio must be at least 100%, meaning the bank can survive a month-long stress scenario using its own liquid assets. RBI phased it in from January 2015 and it reached 100% in 2019.

HQLA are assets that can be turned into cash quickly with little loss of value. Level 1 assets include cash, CRR balances in excess of the requirement, and government securities, counted at full value. In India, banks can also count part of their SLR securities as HQLA through the MSF dip-down and the Facility to Avail Liquidity for LCR (FALLCR). Level 2A and 2B assets, such as high-rated corporate bonds, are counted after haircuts and within caps.

Net cash outflows assume that a share of deposits will run off: a small percentage for stable retail deposits, more for less stable deposits and much more for wholesale corporate funding. Expected inflows, capped at 75% of outflows, are deducted. RBI revised run-off factors in 2024-25, including higher rates for deposits that can be withdrawn instantly through digital banking; check RBI for current factors (as of 2026).
LCR works alongside the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), which looks at a one-year horizon and stable funding of long-term assets. Exam tip: LCR = short-term (30 days), NSFR = longer-term (one year).
items.example: A bank holds HQLA of ₹25,000 crore. Expected 30-day outflows under stress: retail deposits ₹1,50,000 crore × 7.5% run-off = ₹11,250 crore; corporate deposits ₹40,000 crore × 40% = ₹16,000 crore; other outflows ₹3,000 crore. Total = ₹30,250 crore. Expected inflows are ₹8,000 crore (below the 75% cap). Net outflows = ₹22,250 crore. LCR = 25,000/22,250 = 112.4%, above the 100% minimum.
faqs: What is the difference between LCR and SLR?

SLR is a statutory requirement under the Banking Regulation Act to hold a fixed percentage of NDTL in liquid assets. LCR is a Basel III ratio based on a stress test of 30-day net outflows. SLR is a simple percentage; LCR depends on the bank's deposit mix. Some SLR securities count towards LCR.
Why did RBI raise run-off factors for digitally enabled deposits?

Mobile and internet banking let depositors move large sums instantly, as seen in some overseas bank runs. RBI therefore proposed higher run-off assumptions for retail deposits with internet and mobile banking access, so banks hold more liquid assets against the risk of faster withdrawals during stress.

items.title: NEFT Meaning: How National Electronic Funds Transfer Works
items.description: NEFT is RBI's nationwide system for bank-to-bank transfers settled in half-hourly batches, 24x7. Learn timings, limits, IFSC use and NEFT vs RTGS here.
items.short: NEFT is a nationwide electronic payment system run by RBI that transfers funds between bank accounts in batches settled every half hour, round the clock.
body: NEFT was launched by RBI in November 2005. Since 16 December 2019 it operates 24x7, all 365 days, including holidays. Transactions are settled in half-hourly batches, 48 batches a day. The sender needs the beneficiary's name, account number and the branch IFSC (Indian Financial System Code), an 11-character code identifying the bank branch.

RBI has not set any minimum or maximum amount for NEFT, though banks may impose their own limits for online transfers. RBI has asked banks not to charge savings account customers for online NEFT transactions; charges for branch-initiated transfers are capped. Even people without a bank account can deposit cash at a branch to send up to ₹50,000 per transaction through NEFT, subject to KYC details.

If a beneficiary bank cannot credit the account, it must return the funds within two hours of the batch settlement. If credit is delayed, the bank must pay penal interest at the current RBI LAF repo rate plus 2% for the delay. Customers get an SMS or email once the credit is confirmed (positive confirmation).

NEFT is the go-to choice for most routine payments like rent or vendor payments. It differs from RTGS, which settles each transaction individually and in real time, and from IMPS and UPI, which are run by NPCI and credit almost instantly.
items.example: Ravi sends ₹45,000 rent through NEFT at 10:12 pm on a Sunday. The transaction joins the 10:30 pm batch; the landlord's account is credited soon after settlement, typically within an hour. Had the beneficiary account number been wrong, the money would be returned within two hours of the batch. If credit were delayed by two days without reason, the bank would owe interest at repo + 2%; at 7.5%, that is 45,000 × 7.5% × 2/365 = about ₹18.
faqs: Is there a minimum amount for NEFT?

No. RBI has not prescribed any minimum or maximum amount for NEFT transactions. You can send ₹1 or ₹1 crore. Banks may set their own per-day or per-transaction limits for internet and mobile banking based on risk, and cash-based remittances by walk-in customers are capped at ₹50,000 per transaction.
Does NEFT work on bank holidays?

Yes. Since December 2019 NEFT is available 24x7, including Sundays and bank holidays. Batches run every half hour around the clock. Earlier it worked only on working days during set hours, which is why some older textbooks mention fixed timings.

items.title: RTGS Meaning: Real Time Gross Settlement Limit and Rules
items.description: RTGS settles high-value bank transfers individually and in real time. Learn the ₹2 lakh minimum, 24x7 timings, charges and how RTGS differs from NEFT.
items.short: RTGS is RBI's payment system for transferring funds between banks on a real-time, transaction-by-transaction basis, used mainly for high-value payments of ₹2 lakh and above.
body: 'Real time' means the payment is processed as soon as it is received, not held for a batch. 'Gross settlement' means each transaction is settled individually, not netted against others. Once settled in RBI's books, the payment is final and irrevocable. India started RTGS in March 2004, and since 14 December 2020 it runs 24x7 throughout the year.

The minimum amount for RTGS is ₹2 lakh; there is no upper limit set by RBI. It is therefore the preferred route for property payments, large business transactions and inter-bank settlements. Banks must credit the beneficiary within 30 minutes of receiving the message; if they cannot, the funds must be returned within one hour of receipt. RBI has waived charges on online RTGS transactions by savings account holders, and branch charges are capped (check RBI for current rules as of 2026).

Because RTGS settles in central bank money in real time, it removes settlement risk, which is crucial for large payments. Banks maintain current accounts with RBI and need enough balance to settle each transaction; RBI provides intra-day liquidity against collateral to keep payments flowing.
Exam traps: RTGS has a minimum (₹2 lakh) but no maximum; NEFT has neither. RTGS settles individually; NEFT settles in half-hourly batches. Both are run by RBI, while IMPS and UPI are run by NPCI.
items.example: Meena pays ₹18 lakh to a builder for a flat booking. NEFT would also work, but RTGS gives immediate settlement and confirmation. She initiates it at 8:40 pm; the builder's bank receives and credits it within minutes. A payment of ₹1.5 lakh could not go through RTGS because it is below the ₹2 lakh minimum; it would use NEFT or IMPS instead.
faqs: What is the minimum and maximum amount for RTGS?

The minimum amount for an RTGS transaction is ₹2 lakh. RBI has not set any upper limit, though banks may set their own caps for online channels based on risk management. Amounts below ₹2 lakh should be sent through NEFT, IMPS or UPI.
Can an RTGS payment be reversed?

Once RTGS settles in RBI's books, it is final and irrevocable. The sender's bank cannot pull it back. If money went to a wrong account, the sender must request the beneficiary's bank to contact the account holder, and return depends on the recipient's consent or legal action.

items.title: IMPS Meaning: Immediate Payment Service, Limit and Use
items.description: IMPS is NPCI's 24x7 instant interbank transfer service via mobile, internet, ATM or branch. Learn the ₹5 lakh limit, MMID method and how it differs from NEFT.
items.short: IMPS is an instant, round-the-clock interbank fund transfer service operated by NPCI, available through mobile banking, internet banking, ATMs, SMS and bank branches.
body: IMPS was launched by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) in November 2010, initially as a mobile payment system. It credits the beneficiary almost immediately, 24x7, including holidays, which was a big advance when NEFT worked only in batches on working days.

Funds can be sent in several ways: using the beneficiary's account number and IFSC; using their mobile number plus MMID (Mobile Money Identifier, a 7-digit code linked to their account); or, in newer versions, using the mobile number and bank name alone. The per-transaction limit was raised by RBI to ₹5 lakh in 2021, though banks set their own limits within this (check as of 2026).

Unlike NEFT and RTGS, which RBI runs and settles in central bank money, IMPS is a retail system run by NPCI, with transactions cleared instantly and settled between banks in multiple cycles. Banks can levy small charges for IMPS; many offer it free on digital channels.

IMPS is also the backbone that UPI was built on. UPI added the virtual payment address (like name@bank) and a common app interface. Exam questions often ask which organisation runs IMPS (NPCI), its launch year (2010) and its current limit.
items.example: At 11:45 pm on a Saturday, Ankit transfers ₹25,000 to his sister for a hostel fee due the next morning. Using IMPS with her account number and IFSC, the money reaches her account within seconds. If he used NEFT, it would go in the 12:00 midnight batch and usually still arrive quickly. But for ₹6 lakh, IMPS would not work (above the ₹5 lakh cap), so he would use NEFT or RTGS.
faqs: Who operates IMPS in India?

IMPS is operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), an umbrella organisation for retail payments set up by RBI and the Indian Banks' Association in 2008. NPCI also runs UPI, RuPay, NACH, AePS and the cheque truncation system. NEFT and RTGS are run directly by RBI.
What is MMID in IMPS?

MMID or Mobile Money Identifier is a seven-digit number issued by a bank and linked to a customer's mobile number and account. A sender can transfer money using the recipient's mobile number and MMID instead of account number and IFSC. With UPI's spread, MMID use has declined but it remains a valid IMPS method.

items.title: What is UPI? Unified Payments Interface Meaning and Working
items.description: UPI is NPCI's instant payment system that links bank accounts to mobile apps using a VPA and UPI PIN. Learn how it works, limits, UPI Lite and safety tips.
items.short: Unified Payments Interface is an instant real-time payment system developed by NPCI that lets users send and receive money between bank accounts through a mobile app using a virtual address.
body: UPI was launched in April 2016 and went public in August 2016. It lets a user link one or more bank accounts to a UPI app such as BHIM, a bank's own app or a third-party app. Each user gets a Virtual Payment Address (VPA) or UPI ID, like ravi@okbank, so payments can be made without sharing account numbers. Payments are authorised with a UPI PIN, set by the user.

Behind the scenes, UPI runs on the IMPS rails and settles between banks through NPCI. It supports person-to-person (P2P) transfers, person-to-merchant (P2M) payments via QR codes, collect requests, AutoPay mandates for subscriptions, and UPI Lite for small payments without a PIN. RuPay credit cards and pre-sanctioned credit lines can also be linked.

The standard limit is ₹1 lakh per transaction, with higher limits for specific categories such as tax payments, hospitals, education and IPO applications, and banks may set lower daily limits. Limits change, so check NPCI or your bank (as of 2026). Most P2P and P2M payments from bank accounts are free for users.

Safety points examiners and banks stress: you never need to enter a UPI PIN to receive money, only to pay. A 'collect request' from a stranger saying you have won a prize is a common fraud. UPI is also expanding abroad through links with payment systems in Singapore, UAE, France and other countries.
items.example: Priya buys groceries worth ₹640 by scanning the shop's QR code; she enters her UPI PIN and the shop gets an instant credit. For a ₹150 tea bill she uses UPI Lite, which doesn't need a PIN. When her friend sends a 'collect request' of ₹2,000 for a shared cab, she approves and enters her PIN. But a stranger's request saying 'Enter PIN to receive ₹5,000 cashback' is a scam: entering the PIN would debit ₹5,000.
faqs: Do I need to enter UPI PIN to receive money?

No. Receiving money through UPI never requires a PIN. The PIN is only for authorising a debit from your account. Any message or call asking you to enter your PIN to receive a refund, prize or cashback is a fraud, and you should decline the request and report it to your bank.
What is UPI Lite?

UPI Lite is an on-device wallet within UPI apps for small-value payments without entering a UPI PIN. You load money from your bank account into it, and payments up to a set amount debit the Lite balance. It reduces load on bank servers and failures for small transactions. Limits are set by NPCI and RBI.

items.title: What is a Cheque? Meaning, Parties, Types and Validity
items.description: A cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on a bank and payable on demand. Learn the parties, bearer vs order cheques, the 3-month validity and common mistakes.
items.short: A cheque is a written, signed instruction by an account holder ordering a specified bank to pay a certain sum of money on demand to a named person or to the bearer.
body: Section 6 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 defines a cheque as a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand. The Act's 2002 amendment also recognised electronic cheques and truncated cheques. There are three parties: the drawer (who writes it), the drawee (the bank on which it is drawn) and the payee (who receives the money).

Types by payee: a bearer cheque is payable to whoever presents it, so it is risky if lost; an order cheque (where 'or bearer' is struck off) is payable only to the named payee or someone to whom he endorses it. A crossed cheque is payable only through a bank account, not across the counter. A self cheque lets the drawer withdraw cash. A post-dated cheque carries a future date and cannot be paid before it; a stale cheque is one presented after its validity.

RBI reduced cheque validity to three months from the date written on it, effective 1 April 2012. Banks follow CTS-2010 standards for cheque format, with features like a pantograph 'VOID' mark and UV logo to prevent fraud. Under the Positive Pay System, customers re-confirm key details of cheques above a threshold (₹50,000 onwards, mandatory at many banks for ₹5 lakh and above) before payment.

Common confusions: the drawee is always a bank, never a person. A cheque is not legal tender; the payee may refuse it. Alterations on the cheque, other than the date, are not allowed under CTS rules; a fresh cheque must be issued.
items.example: On 10 January Suresh writes a cheque for ₹38,500 to 'Neha Traders or bearer'. Suresh is the drawer, his bank (say Bank of Baroda, Pune branch) is the drawee and Neha Traders is the payee. If Suresh strikes off 'or bearer', it becomes an order cheque. The cheque is valid until 9 April, three months from its date. Presented on 15 April, it would be returned as stale and Suresh would need to issue a new one.
faqs: How long is a cheque valid in India?

A cheque is valid for three months from the date written on it, as directed by RBI from 1 April 2012. Earlier the validity was six months. After three months the cheque becomes stale and the bank will not pay it. The drawer must revalidate or issue a fresh cheque.
Can a bank pay a post-dated cheque before its date?

No. A post-dated cheque becomes payable only on or after the date written on it. If a bank pays it earlier and the drawer's other cheques bounce meanwhile, the bank may be liable. Also, the drawer can stop payment or close the account before that date.

items.title: Crossed Cheque Meaning: General, Special and A/c Payee
items.description: A crossed cheque can only be paid into a bank account, not in cash. Learn general, special and account payee crossing under the NI Act with simple examples.
items.short: A crossed cheque has two parallel lines drawn across its face, instructing the paying bank to pay the amount only through a bank account and not in cash over the counter.
body: Crossing is covered in Sections 123 to 131 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Its purpose is safety: even if a crossed cheque is lost or stolen, the money can be traced because it must pass through a bank account.

General crossing (Section 123) is two parallel transverse lines, with or without words like '& Co.' or 'not negotiable'. The cheque can be paid to any bank, which then credits the payee's account. Special crossing (Section 124) names a particular bank between the lines, such as 'State Bank of India'; the paying bank will pay only to that named bank. Special crossing gives more protection than general crossing.

'Account payee' or 'A/c payee only' crossing is not defined in the Act but is recognised by banking practice and RBI directions. It tells the collecting bank to credit only the account of the named payee. Because of RBI directions, banks do not credit such cheques to any other account, even if endorsed. 'Not negotiable' crossing means the cheque remains transferable, but the transferee cannot get a better title than the transferor had.

Who can cross? The drawer or the holder can cross a cheque, convert general crossing to special, or add 'not negotiable'. A banker to whom a cheque is specially crossed can cross it again to another bank as its collecting agent. Only the drawer can cancel a crossing ('open' the cheque) with full signature.
items.example: Arun issues a ₹60,000 cheque to Kavita, drawing two parallel lines and writing 'A/c payee'. The cheque is lost and found by Rakesh, who tries to deposit it in his own account. His bank refuses, because an account payee cheque can be credited only to Kavita's account. Had it been a bearer cheque without crossing, Rakesh could have encashed it at the counter, and Arun's ₹60,000 would have been lost.
faqs: What is the difference between general and special crossing?

General crossing has only two parallel lines (with or without '& Co.') and allows payment through any bank. Special crossing names a specific bank, and the paying bank will pay only to that bank. Special crossing is safer because it limits the channel through which the cheque can be collected.
Can a crossed cheque be cashed at the counter?

No. A crossed cheque must be paid into a bank account, so the paying bank will not hand over cash. Only the drawer can cancel the crossing by writing 'pay cash' and signing in full, which turns it into an open cheque that can be encashed at the counter.

items.title: Cheque Truncation System (CTS): How Image Clearing Works
items.description: CTS clears cheques using scanned images instead of moving paper. Learn how CTS works, CTS-2010 standards, Positive Pay and why clearing became faster.
items.short: Cheque Truncation System is an image-based cheque clearing system where the physical cheque stops at the collecting bank and only its electronic image and data travel to the paying bank.
body: 'Truncation' means stopping the movement of the paper cheque somewhere along the clearing chain. Under CTS, the presenting bank scans the cheque and sends the image along with MICR data (the magnetic code at the bottom, including cheque number, bank and branch codes) to the clearing house, which forwards it to the drawee bank for payment. The 2002 amendment to the NI Act gave legal recognition to truncated cheques.

RBI piloted CTS in New Delhi in 2008, then rolled it out to Chennai and Mumbai, and by September 2021 brought all bank branches in the country under three grids. CTS is operated by NPCI. It removed the cost and delay of physically moving cheques, cut frauds involving tampering in transit and allowed faster credit.

To work with CTS, cheques must follow the CTS-2010 standard: specific paper with a watermark, a 'VOID' pantograph that appears on photocopies, a UV-visible bank logo, and fixed field positions. Changes on the cheque (except date) are not permitted. RBI's Positive Pay System, launched in 2021, lets the drawer pre-share details like date, amount and payee name, which the paying bank matches before paying high-value cheques.

RBI has moved CTS from batch clearing to continuous clearing with settlement on realisation, in phases from October 2025, aiming for same-day credit within hours. Check RBI for the latest timelines (as of 2026).
items.example: Sneha deposits a ₹1,20,000 cheque drawn on an HDFC Bank branch into her SBI account. SBI scans it and sends the image plus MICR data to the CTS grid. HDFC Bank checks the image, signature and Positive Pay details that the drawer had entered earlier (amount ₹1,20,000, payee Sneha), finds a match, and confirms payment. Sneha's account is credited without the paper cheque ever leaving SBI.
faqs: Why are corrections on a cheque not allowed under CTS?

In image-based clearing, the paying bank sees only a scan, so it cannot easily verify whether a change was made by the drawer or a fraudster. To reduce risk, RBI directed that no changes or corrections be made on CTS cheques, except to the date with the drawer's authentication. Any other correction requires a fresh cheque.
What is the Positive Pay System?

Positive Pay is a fraud-prevention mechanism for cheques. The drawer shares key details such as cheque number, date, amount and payee name with their bank through SMS, app or net banking. When the cheque is presented in CTS, these details are matched. Banks can make it mandatory for cheques of ₹5 lakh and above.

items.title: Cheque Bounce Section 138 NI Act: Process, Timeline, Penalty
items.description: Section 138 of the NI Act makes dishonour of a cheque for insufficient funds an offence. Learn the 30-15-30 day timeline, penalty and key conditions.
items.short: Cheque bounce under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is the criminal offence of a cheque, issued to discharge a legally enforceable debt, being returned unpaid for insufficient funds.
body: The offence applies when a cheque is dishonoured because the amount in the account is insufficient or exceeds the arrangement with the bank. Courts have extended it to dishonour due to 'account closed' and 'payment stopped by drawer' where the intention was to avoid payment. It does not apply to cheques given as gifts, donations or security where no debt exists at the time of presentation, though courts examine this case by case.

Conditions and timeline: the cheque must be presented within its validity (three months). After dishonour, the payee must send a written demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving information from the bank. The drawer gets 15 days from receipt of notice to pay. If he does not, the payee must file a complaint before a Judicial Magistrate within one month after the 15-day period ends. Courts may condone delay for sufficient cause.

Punishment: imprisonment up to two years, or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. The court may order interim compensation of up to 20% of the cheque amount under Section 143A (added in 2018). The offence is compoundable, meaning parties can settle at any stage. The law presumes the cheque was issued for a debt (Section 139), so the drawer must prove otherwise.

Banks also act: if cheques of ₹1 crore or more bounce four times in a financial year due to insufficient funds, banks are required to stop issuing a new cheque book and may close the account at their discretion.
items.example: Ramesh gives a supplier a ₹2,00,000 cheque dated 1 March. It bounces on 10 March; the supplier gets the bank's return memo on 12 March. The demand notice must be sent by 11 April (30 days). Ramesh receives it on 15 April and has until 30 April to pay. If he doesn't, the complaint must be filed by 30 May. If convicted, he could face up to two years in prison or a fine up to ₹4,00,000, or both.
faqs: Is a cheque bounce a criminal case or a civil case?

It can be both. Section 138 makes it a criminal offence with possible imprisonment and fine. The payee can also file a civil recovery suit, including a summary suit under Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, to recover the money. Both remedies can be pursued at the same time.
What if the demand notice is not sent within 30 days?

The complaint under Section 138 will fail because notice within 30 days of receiving the bank's information is a mandatory condition. However, the payee can present the cheque again within its validity period and, on fresh dishonour, send a new notice in time. Civil recovery of the debt also remains available.

items.title: SARFAESI Act 2002: Meaning, Section 13 Notice and Process
items.description: SARFAESI lets banks enforce security on NPAs without court intervention. Learn the Section 13(2) 60-day notice, exemptions, borrower remedies and an example.
items.short: The SARFAESI Act lets banks and financial institutions take possession of and sell the security of a defaulting borrower, without going to court, once the loan has become an NPA.
body: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 has three pillars: securitisation of financial assets, reconstruction of assets through asset reconstruction companies (ARCs), and enforcement of security interest by secured creditors. It was passed because civil court recovery took years, and even the DRT system was slow.

Process: once the account is classified as NPA, the secured creditor issues a demand notice under Section 13(2), giving the borrower 60 days to repay the full dues. The borrower may make a representation, which the bank must answer within 15 days. If the borrower fails to pay, under Section 13(4) the bank can take possession of the secured asset, take over management of the business, appoint a manager, or ask anyone who owes money to the borrower to pay the bank instead. The bank can then sell the asset through a public auction after valuation and a 30-day sale notice. Section 14 allows the bank to seek help from the District Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate to get physical possession.

Exemptions: SARFAESI does not apply to agricultural land, loans where the amount due is less than 20% of principal and interest, or security interest for amounts below ₹1 lakh. For consortium loans, creditors holding at least 60% of the outstanding amount must agree.
Borrower's remedy: appeal to the Debt Recovery Tribunal under Section 17 within 45 days of the possession measure, and further to the DRAT.
items.example: A borrower's ₹40 lakh home loan, secured by his flat, turns NPA on 1 July. The bank issues a Section 13(2) notice on 5 July demanding ₹38.5 lakh outstanding. The 60-day period ends on 3 September. With no payment, the bank takes symbolic possession under Section 13(4), then physical possession through the District Magistrate. The flat is auctioned for ₹45 lakh; after dues and costs of ₹39.2 lakh, the bank must return about ₹5.8 lakh to the borrower.
faqs: Can a bank use SARFAESI for any loan?

No. It applies only to secured loans that have been classified as NPA, where the outstanding is at least ₹1 lakh and at least 20% of principal and interest. It cannot be used on agricultural land. Unsecured loans like most personal loans and credit cards cannot be recovered through SARFAESI.
What can a borrower do against a SARFAESI action?

The borrower can make a representation against the Section 13(2) notice, which the bank must answer within 15 days. If the bank takes possession, the borrower or any aggrieved person can appeal to the Debt Recovery Tribunal under Section 17 within 45 days. Paying the full dues before the sale also stops the process.

items.title: Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT): Meaning, Limit and Process
items.description: DRTs are special tribunals for banks to recover debts of ₹20 lakh and above. Learn the RDB Act, DRT vs DRAT, timelines and how DRT links to SARFAESI.
items.short: Debt Recovery Tribunals are special quasi-judicial bodies set up to quickly decide cases filed by banks and financial institutions for recovery of debts above a set threshold.
body: DRTs were created under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, now renamed the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (RDB Act). Before them, banks filed ordinary civil suits that could take decades. The minimum claim for a DRT is ₹20 lakh, raised from ₹10 lakh in 2018; smaller debts go to civil courts or other forums.

A DRT is headed by a Presiding Officer, usually a person qualified to be a District Judge. Appeals from DRT orders go to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) within 30 days; to file an appeal, the borrower must usually deposit 50% of the amount determined by DRT, which the DRAT can reduce to 25%. Further challenges go to the High Court under its writ jurisdiction.

The process: the bank files an Original Application; the tribunal summons the defendant; after hearing, it issues a Recovery Certificate. A Recovery Officer then executes it by attaching and selling property, appointing receivers or even ordering arrest. The Act aims for disposal within 180 days, though actual timelines are often longer due to pending cases.

DRTs have additional roles. Borrowers appeal against SARFAESI actions to the DRT under Section 17 of SARFAESI. Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, DRTs act as the adjudicating authority for insolvency of individuals and partnership firms, while the NCLT handles companies.
items.example: A bank has an unsecured business loan claim of ₹65 lakh against a partnership firm. It files an Original Application in the DRT with jurisdiction. After hearing, the DRT issues a Recovery Certificate for ₹65 lakh plus interest. The firm appeals to DRAT and is told to deposit 50%, or ₹32.5 lakh; the DRAT can reduce this to 25%, ₹16.25 lakh. A claim of only ₹12 lakh could not go to DRT, being below the ₹20 lakh threshold.
faqs: What is the minimum amount for filing a case in DRT?

Banks and financial institutions can approach the DRT for debts of ₹20 lakh and above. The central government raised this limit from ₹10 lakh in 2018 to reduce the load on tribunals. For smaller amounts, banks use civil courts, Lok Adalats or SARFAESI if the loan is secured and eligible.
Is DRT the same as NCLT?

No. DRT handles recovery suits by banks and financial institutions and insolvency of individuals and partnership firms under the IBC. The National Company Law Tribunal handles insolvency of companies and LLPs, plus company law matters. Appeals from DRT go to DRAT, and from NCLT to NCLAT.

items.title: Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC): Meaning and Working
items.description: An ARC buys bad loans from banks and tries to recover or revive them. Learn how ARCs work, security receipts, the 15:85 structure and RBI rules in India.
items.short: An asset reconstruction company is an RBI-registered specialised financial institution that buys non-performing loans from banks at a discount and tries to recover or restructure them.
body: ARCs are set up and registered with RBI under Section 3 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002. India's first, ARCIL, began in 2003. Banks sell NPAs to ARCs to clean their balance sheets and get cash or tradable instruments in return, while ARCs specialise in recovery: restructuring the borrower's business, changing management, rescheduling debt, enforcing security or selling the assets.

In a typical deal, the ARC sets up a trust that buys the NPA from the bank at an agreed price, often well below the outstanding amount. The trust pays the bank partly in cash and partly through security receipts (SRs), which entitle the holder to a share of future recoveries. RBI requires the ARC to invest at least 15% of the SRs issued in each deal, so it has skin in the game; the rest (up to 85%) may be held by the selling bank or other investors. If recoveries exceed the price, SR holders gain; if not, they lose.

RBI raised the minimum net owned fund for ARCs to ₹300 crore in 2022 and has tightened rules on governance and on banks investing in SRs of their own sold loans. These limits may change, so check RBI's master directions (as of 2026).

The National Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (NARCL), sometimes called a 'bad bank', was set up in 2021 with government-guaranteed security receipts to take over large legacy NPAs. Exam traps: ARCs are regulated by RBI, not SEBI; and selling an NPA to an ARC does not waive the borrower's liability, which simply passes to the ARC.
items.example: A bank holds an NPA with ₹500 crore outstanding, fully provided except ₹100 crore. An ARC agrees to buy it for ₹200 crore. It pays 15% (₹30 crore) by investing in SRs itself and issues ₹170 crore of SRs to the bank (in practice deals often include upfront cash). Over five years the ARC recovers ₹260 crore by selling the borrower's factory. After its fees and expenses of ₹20 crore, ₹240 crore is distributed to SR holders, a gain over the ₹200 crore price.
faqs: Who regulates asset reconstruction companies in India?

ARCs are registered and regulated by the Reserve Bank of India under the SARFAESI Act, 2002. RBI sets norms for their capital, investment in security receipts, governance and acquisition of assets. SEBI's role is limited to listed security receipts, where applicable, but the primary regulator is RBI.
Does a borrower's loan get waived when sold to an ARC?

No. When a bank sells an NPA to an ARC, the debt is transferred with all its rights. The borrower still owes the full contractual amount, now to the ARC, which can use SARFAESI, DRT or the IBC to recover it. The discounted price paid by the ARC does not reduce what the borrower owes.

items.title: Wilful Defaulter Meaning: RBI Rules and Consequences
items.description: A wilful defaulter can repay but doesn't, or diverts loan money. Learn RBI's definition, the identification process and penalties like bans on fresh credit.
items.short: A wilful defaulter is a borrower who defaults on repayment to a lender despite having the capacity to pay, or who diverts, siphons off or misuses the borrowed funds.
body: RBI's framework on wilful defaulters, consolidated in its 2024 Master Direction on Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters, lists situations that count as wilful default: not paying despite having the ability; using funds for purposes other than those sanctioned (diversion); siphoning off funds so that they do not exist in the form of assets; and disposing of or removing secured assets without the lender's knowledge. The current threshold for examination is an outstanding amount of ₹25 lakh and above (check RBI's direction as of 2026).

Identification follows a set process. An Identification Committee of senior officials examines the evidence and issues a show-cause notice. The borrower gets 15 days to reply and may be given a personal hearing. A Review Committee headed by the bank's chief executive confirms the decision, after which the name is reported to credit information companies and RBI.

Consequences are severe: no additional credit facilities from any bank or NBFC; a declared wilful defaulter and the company's promoters and whole-time directors are barred from institutional finance for new ventures for a period (five years from removal of the name from the list, under RBI rules) and cannot get restructuring of their loans; lenders may start criminal proceedings and the IBC bars such persons from bidding for stressed assets under Section 29A.

Exam traps: a borrower who cannot pay because the business genuinely failed is a defaulter, not a wilful defaulter. Non-executive and nominee directors are generally not tagged unless shown to have been involved.
items.example: A company borrowed ₹10 crore for a new plant. Audits show it transferred ₹6 crore to a promoter's real-estate firm and stopped paying EMIs, though its main business earned ₹2 crore a year in profit. This is diversion plus default despite capacity. After a show-cause notice and hearing, the bank's committees declare the company and its promoter wilful defaulters. Neither can get fresh loans from any bank or NBFC, and the promoter cannot float a new company for the barred period.
faqs: What is the difference between a defaulter and a wilful defaulter?

A defaulter simply has not repaid on time, often due to genuine business losses or personal hardship. A wilful defaulter has the capacity to pay but refuses, or has diverted or siphoned the loan money, or disposed of security without permission. Only the latter faces the special bans and reporting under RBI's framework.
Can a borrower challenge a wilful defaulter tag?

Yes. RBI's process requires a show-cause notice, a chance to reply within 15 days and a personal hearing where appropriate, followed by a reasoned order reviewed by a senior committee. A borrower who believes the process was flawed can approach a High Court through a writ petition.

items.title: CASA Ratio Meaning: Formula and Why Banks Chase It
items.description: CASA ratio is the share of current and savings account deposits in a bank's total deposits. Learn the formula, why low-cost deposits boost margins, example.
items.short: CASA ratio is the share of a bank's total deposits that comes from current accounts and savings accounts, which are its cheapest sources of funds.
body: Formula: CASA ratio = (Current account deposits + Savings account deposits) ÷ Total deposits × 100. Current accounts, used by businesses for daily transactions, pay no interest. Savings accounts pay a low rate, deregulated by RBI in 2011 and typically much lower than fixed deposit rates. Term deposits (fixed and recurring) cost more.

A high CASA ratio means a lower average cost of funds, which lets the bank either lend more cheaply or earn a higher net interest margin. That is why banks invest heavily in branch networks, salary account tie-ups, digital banking and transaction services: CASA deposits come from customers who use the bank daily, not those shopping for the best rate.

CASA is also considered a stable, sticky funding source in normal times, though digital banking has made savings balances more mobile. Private banks with strong retail franchises often report CASA ratios around 40% or more, while some newer banks rely more on term deposits. When interest rates rise, customers tend to shift money from savings to fixed deposits, and CASA ratios fall across the industry.
Common mistake: CASA is a ratio of deposits, not of total liabilities or loans. Also, a high CASA ratio alone does not mean a bank is healthy; asset quality and capital also matter.
items.example: A bank has current deposits of ₹40,000 crore (0% interest), savings deposits of ₹60,000 crore at 2.75%, and term deposits of ₹1,50,000 crore at 7%. Total deposits = ₹2,50,000 crore. CASA ratio = 1,00,000/2,50,000 = 40%. Interest cost = 0 + 1,650 + 10,500 = ₹12,150 crore, an average cost of 4.86%. If CASA were 30% (₹75,000 crore, split in the same 40:60 ratio) the average cost would rise to about 5.395%.
faqs: Why do banks want a high CASA ratio?

Current accounts pay no interest and savings accounts pay little, so a higher CASA share lowers the bank's average cost of deposits. Cheaper funds mean better margins or more competitive loan rates. CASA customers also bring fee income from transactions and cross-selling opportunities, making them valuable relationships.
Does a fixed deposit count in CASA?

No. Fixed deposits and recurring deposits are term deposits and are excluded from CASA. However, some banks offer sweep-in accounts where surplus savings balance is moved into a fixed deposit automatically; the swept portion is generally reported as a term deposit, not CASA.

items.title: Net Interest Margin (NIM): Formula and Bank Example
items.description: NIM measures a bank's net interest income as a share of its interest-earning assets. Learn the formula, what drives NIM in India and a worked example.
items.short: Net interest margin is a bank's interest earned minus interest paid, expressed as a percentage of its average interest-earning assets, showing how profitably it lends.
body: Formula: NIM = (Interest income − Interest expense) ÷ Average interest-earning assets × 100. The numerator is net interest income (NII). Interest-earning assets include loans, investments in bonds and inter-bank placements. Some analysts use total assets instead, so check the definition when comparing.

NIM is the core profitability measure for banks because lending is their main business. In India, NIMs typically fall roughly in a band of about 2.5% to 4.5% depending on the bank's business mix. Drivers include: the CASA ratio (cheaper deposits lift NIM); the loan mix (unsecured retail and microfinance loans earn more than corporate loans); asset quality (interest on NPAs is not recognised, so high NPAs reduce NIM); and the rate cycle.

With most retail loans now linked to the external repo benchmark, loan rates reprice quickly after an RBI rate change, while fixed deposit rates change only when deposits renew. So when RBI cuts rates, NIMs often shrink in the short term; when it hikes, NIMs often widen first.

NIM differs from spread. Spread is the yield on advances minus the cost of deposits, two rates subtracted from each other. NIM uses income and expense amounts over the asset base, so it also reflects how much of the balance sheet earns interest and how it is funded.
items.example: A bank's average interest-earning assets are ₹3,00,000 crore. It earns interest of ₹25,500 crore and pays ₹15,300 crore on deposits and borrowings. NII = ₹10,200 crore. NIM = 10,200/3,00,000 = 3.4%. If a repo cut lowers loan yields by 0.25% on half the assets (₹1,50,000 crore) before deposit costs fall, income drops by ₹375 crore and NIM falls to 9,825/3,00,000 = 3.275%.
faqs: Why do bank NIMs fall when RBI cuts the repo rate?

Most retail and MSE loans are linked to the repo rate and reprice within three months, while fixed deposits keep their old rates until maturity. So interest income falls faster than interest expense, compressing NIM temporarily. As deposits renew at lower rates, margins usually recover partly.
Is a higher NIM always better?

A higher NIM generally means more profitable lending, but it may come from riskier loans, such as unsecured personal loans or microfinance, that can produce higher credit losses later. Analysts look at NIM together with credit costs, asset quality and return on assets to judge real profitability.

items.term: Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR)
items.title: MCLR Meaning: Marginal Cost of Funds Lending Rate Explained
items.description: MCLR is the internal benchmark lending rate banks used from 2016, built on the marginal cost of funds. Learn its components, reset rules and MCLR vs EBLR.
items.short: MCLR is an internal benchmark lending rate, introduced by RBI in April 2016, that each bank calculates from its marginal cost of funds and below which it generally cannot lend.
body: Before MCLR, banks used the base rate system (2010), which relied on average cost of funds. Because old deposits at higher rates kept the average high, RBI rate cuts reached borrowers slowly. MCLR was designed to improve transmission by using the marginal cost, the rate at which the bank raises fresh money today.

MCLR has four components: the marginal cost of funds (marginal cost of borrowings and return on net worth); the negative carry on CRR (the cost of keeping idle cash with RBI); operating costs; and a tenor premium for longer-tenure loans. Banks publish MCLRs for different tenors, such as overnight, one month, three months, six months and one year, and review them every month.

A loan's rate is MCLR plus a spread, and the rate resets periodically, typically once a year for home loans linked to the one-year MCLR. So even if MCLR falls this month, your rate may change only at the next reset date.

Transmission under MCLR remained slow, so from 1 October 2019 RBI made it mandatory for banks to link all new floating-rate personal, retail and MSE loans to an external benchmark like the repo rate. MCLR still applies to many corporate loans and to older retail loans, and borrowers can switch to an external benchmark on mutually agreed terms.
items.example: A bank's one-year MCLR is 8.85%. Priya's home loan is priced at MCLR + 0.40% = 9.25% with an annual reset in March. In May the bank cuts one-year MCLR to 8.60%, but Priya's rate stays 9.25% until March. At the reset it falls to 9.00%. On an outstanding loan of ₹40 lakh, that saves about 0.25% × 40,00,000 = ₹10,000 of interest in the first year after reset.
faqs: What is the difference between MCLR and base rate?

Base rate, used from 2010 to 2016, was calculated on the average cost of funds, so it moved slowly when interest rates changed. MCLR uses the marginal cost of fresh funds and is reviewed monthly, making it more responsive. Both are internal benchmarks set by the bank itself, unlike external benchmarks.
Should MCLR borrowers switch to a repo-linked loan?

That depends on the spread offered, switching fees and the borrower's view of rates; no single answer fits everyone. Repo-linked loans pass on RBI rate changes faster in both directions, while MCLR loans adjust only at reset. Borrowers should compare the effective rate and costs offered by their bank.

items.title: External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR): Repo-Linked Loans
items.description: EBLR links floating-rate loans to an external benchmark like RBI's repo rate. Learn the 2019 rule, allowed benchmarks, reset frequency and a worked example.
items.short: External Benchmark Lending Rate is a floating loan rate linked to an outside benchmark, such as RBI's repo rate or a treasury bill yield, plus a spread, instead of the bank's internal rate.
body: From 1 October 2019, RBI made it mandatory for banks to link all new floating-rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto, education, personal) and floating-rate loans to micro and small enterprises to an external benchmark. Banks may choose one of four: the RBI policy repo rate, the Government of India 3-month treasury bill yield, the 6-month treasury bill yield published by FBIL, or any other benchmark yield published by FBIL. Most banks chose the repo rate, so these loans are popularly called repo-linked lending rate (RLLR) loans.

Loan rate = External benchmark + Spread. The spread has two parts: the bank's operating cost and credit risk premium. The credit risk premium can change only if the borrower's credit profile changes substantially, as agreed in the loan contract. The interest rate must be reset at least once every three months.

The main benefit is transparency and faster transmission. When the MPC changes repo, every repo-linked loan reprices at its next reset, in both directions. The borrower can see exactly why the rate changed. In 2023 RBI also required banks to give borrowers the choice of increasing EMI, extending tenure, or both when rates rise, and to share clear information on the reset.
Exam point: EBLR is mandatory for new floating loans in the specified categories; MCLR continues for other loans and older accounts. NBFCs are not covered by the EBLR mandate.
items.example: A bank links its home loans to repo. With repo at 5.50% and a spread of 2.60%, the loan rate is 8.10%. For a ₹50 lakh, 20-year loan, the EMI is about ₹42,134. If MPC cuts repo by 0.25%, the rate becomes 7.85% at the next quarterly reset, and the EMI on the same balance and remaining tenure falls to about ₹41,356, roughly ₹778 lower each month.
faqs: Which external benchmarks can banks use?

RBI allows four: the policy repo rate, the 3-month Government of India treasury bill yield published by FBIL, the 6-month treasury bill yield published by FBIL, and any other benchmark market interest rate published by FBIL. A bank must use a uniform benchmark within a loan category for transparency.
How often does a repo-linked loan rate change?

The rate must be reset at least once every three months under RBI rules. Banks usually reset on the first day of the month or quarter after an MPC decision. Between resets the rate stays the same even if the repo rate changes, so the full effect appears only at the next reset date.

items.title: Deposit Insurance DICGC: ₹5 Lakh Cover Explained
items.description: DICGC insures bank deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank. Learn what is covered, excluded, how the limit applies across accounts and claim timelines.
items.short: Deposit insurance protects bank depositors by paying them up to a fixed limit if their bank fails; in India it is provided by DICGC, a wholly owned subsidiary of RBI.
body: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) was formed in 1978 by merging the Deposit Insurance Corporation (1962) and the Credit Guarantee Corporation. It insures deposits in all commercial banks including foreign banks' branches in India, local area banks, small finance banks, payments banks, regional rural banks and co-operative banks. It does not cover NBFCs.

The limit is ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, covering principal and interest together, raised from ₹1 lakh with effect from 4 February 2020. Savings, current, fixed and recurring deposits are all covered. Excluded are deposits of central and state governments, foreign governments, inter-bank deposits, and deposits of state land development banks with state co-operative banks. Banks pay the premium (not depositors), and it cannot be passed on to customers. The limit may be revised, so check DICGC (as of 2026).

Key rule: deposits held in the 'same capacity and same right' at all branches of one bank are added together. So two FDs in your name at two branches of the same bank share one ₹5 lakh cover. But deposits in different capacities, such as your individual account and a joint account with your spouse, or a deposit as a partner of a firm, are insured separately.
After the DICGC (Amendment) Act, 2021, depositors of a bank placed under RBI moratorium can get up to ₹5 lakh within about 90 days, instead of waiting for liquidation, which used to take years.
items.example: Anita has a savings account with ₹1.2 lakh and an FD of ₹4.5 lakh plus ₹30,000 accrued interest in Bank A, all in her sole name. Total = ₹6 lakh, but cover is ₹5 lakh, so ₹1 lakh is uninsured. She also has a joint FD of ₹3 lakh with her husband in Bank A, insured separately up to ₹5 lakh. Her ₹4 lakh FD in Bank B is fully covered. If Bank A failed, she would receive ₹5 lakh + ₹3 lakh = ₹8 lakh from DICGC.
faqs: Is my fixed deposit in an NBFC covered by DICGC?

No. DICGC covers only deposits in banks, including commercial, small finance, payments, regional rural and co-operative banks. Deposits with NBFCs, housing finance companies or corporate fixed deposits are not insured by DICGC, which is one of the key differences between a bank deposit and an NBFC deposit.
Who pays the deposit insurance premium?

The insured bank pays the premium to DICGC, currently a flat rate on its assessable deposits, and must not recover it from depositors. RBI and DICGC have discussed moving to a risk-based premium where riskier banks pay more. Depositors do not pay anything directly for this protection.

items.title: Demand Draft (DD) Meaning: How It Differs from a Cheque
items.description: A demand draft is a prepaid instrument issued by a bank, payable on demand. Learn parties, validity, the ₹50,000 cash rule, and DD vs cheque differences.
items.short: A demand draft is a prepaid negotiable instrument issued by a bank, ordering its own branch or correspondent to pay a specified sum to a named payee on demand.
body: The customer who wants to pay (the purchaser) gives the bank cash or a debit to their account plus a commission, and the bank issues the draft. Because the bank has already collected the money, a DD cannot bounce for lack of funds, which is why colleges, government offices and examination bodies have traditionally asked for DDs.

Parties: the drawer is the issuing bank branch, the drawee is the paying branch (often of the same bank), and the payee is the person named. Unlike a cheque, the purchaser is not a party to the instrument. A DD is always an order instrument and is usually crossed 'account payee', so it is credited to the payee's account.

Rules to remember: like cheques, DDs are valid for three months from the date of issue; after that they must be revalidated. Under RBI's KYC directions, a DD of ₹50,000 or more must be issued only by debit to the customer's account or against a cheque, not against cash. Since September 2018, RBI requires the purchaser's name to be printed on the face of the draft to improve traceability. If a DD is lost, the bank issues a duplicate against an indemnity, after checking the original has not been paid.

DD vs pay order (banker's cheque): a pay order is payable only in the same city where it is issued, while a DD is typically payable at another city. With NEFT, RTGS and UPI available 24x7, DDs are now used mainly where an institution insists on them.
items.example: Kiran needs to pay ₹75,000 as admission fee to a college in Bengaluru that accepts only a DD. She asks her bank in Indore for a draft payable at Bengaluru. Since the amount exceeds ₹50,000, the bank debits her savings account instead of taking cash. It charges a commission, say ₹3 per ₹1,000 with a minimum of ₹50, which is ₹225. The DD, crossed 'A/c payee', is valid for three months from issue.
faqs: Can a demand draft bounce like a cheque?

Not for insufficient funds, because the bank collects the money upfront before issuing the draft. A DD may still be returned for technical reasons such as being stale (over three months old), mutilated, or having a mismatch in the payee name. In such cases it is revalidated or reissued by the bank.
What is the difference between a DD and a cheque?

A cheque is drawn by an account holder on his bank and can bounce if funds are short. A DD is drawn by a bank on itself or its branch, prepaid by the purchaser, so payment is assured. A cheque can be bearer or order; a DD is always payable to order.

items.title: Bank Guarantee Meaning: Types, Parties and Example
items.description: A bank guarantee is a bank's promise to pay a beneficiary if its customer fails to perform or pay. Learn financial vs performance guarantees and invocation.
items.short: A bank guarantee is a written promise by a bank to pay a specified amount to a beneficiary if the bank's customer fails to meet a contractual obligation or payment.
body: Legally, a guarantee is a 'contract of guarantee' under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. There are three parties: the applicant or principal debtor (the bank's customer), the beneficiary (who receives the guarantee) and the guarantor (the bank). The bank charges a commission and usually takes security or margin money from its customer, because paying out under the guarantee creates a loan to the customer.

Types: a financial guarantee covers a payment obligation, for example that a buyer will pay a supplier. A performance guarantee covers completion of work or delivery, common in government contracts and construction. A bid bond (earnest money guarantee) assures that a bidder will sign the contract if selected. An advance payment guarantee protects a buyer who pays upfront. A deferred payment guarantee covers instalments for machinery bought on credit.

Most bank guarantees in India are unconditional: the bank must pay on the beneficiary's written demand within the validity and claim period, without investigating the underlying dispute. Courts intervene only in rare cases of egregious fraud or irretrievable injustice. Guarantees have a validity period plus a claim period, and Section 28 of the Contract Act allows a claim period of not less than one year.

Since a guarantee is not a funded loan, it is an off-balance sheet (non-fund based) exposure, but banks still hold capital against it. Exam trap: in a letter of credit the bank is the primary payer; in a bank guarantee it pays only if the customer defaults.
items.example: A road contractor wins a ₹50 crore government project that needs a 5% performance guarantee. Its bank issues a guarantee of ₹2.5 crore in favour of the state PWD, valid for three years plus a one-year claim period. The bank charges 1.5% a year, about ₹3.75 lakh annually, and keeps a 20% margin (₹50 lakh) as fixed deposit. If the contractor abandons work, the PWD invokes the guarantee, the bank pays ₹2.5 crore, and the contractor now owes the bank.
faqs: What is the difference between a bank guarantee and a letter of credit?

Under a letter of credit, the bank pays the seller when the seller presents documents showing it has fulfilled the terms, so the bank is the primary paymaster. Under a bank guarantee, the bank pays only if its customer fails to perform or pay. An LC facilitates a transaction; a guarantee protects against default.
Can a bank refuse to pay an invoked guarantee because the customer disputes it?

Generally no. An unconditional bank guarantee is an independent contract, and the bank must honour a valid demand made within the terms, regardless of disputes between the customer and beneficiary. Courts stop payment only in exceptional cases of established fraud known to the bank or irretrievable harm.

items.title: Letter of Credit (LC): Meaning, Parties, Types, Example
items.description: A letter of credit is a bank undertaking to pay a seller against compliant documents. Learn the parties, sight vs usance LC, UCP 600 and a worked example.
items.short: A letter of credit is a written undertaking by a bank, issued on behalf of a buyer, to pay the seller a stated amount on presenting documents that comply with the LC's terms.
body: LCs solve a trust problem in trade, especially international trade. The exporter does not want to ship goods without payment certainty, and the importer does not want to pay before goods are shipped. With an LC, a bank steps in: the seller ships, presents the required documents (invoice, bill of lading, insurance, certificate of origin) and gets paid by the bank if the documents match the LC terms exactly.

Parties: the applicant (buyer or importer), the beneficiary (seller or exporter), the issuing bank (buyer's bank), the advising bank (in the seller's country, which authenticates and passes on the LC), and sometimes a confirming bank, which adds its own payment undertaking, and a negotiating bank, which examines documents and pays the seller.

Types: a sight LC pays on presentation of documents; a usance or deferred payment LC pays after a set period, such as 90 days after the bill of lading date. LCs under UCP 600 are irrevocable by default. A confirmed LC adds a second bank's guarantee. A revolving LC covers repeated shipments; a back-to-back LC is opened by a trader on the strength of another LC; a standby LC works more like a guarantee.

International LCs are governed by the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (UCP 600) of the International Chamber of Commerce. The golden rule is that banks deal in documents, not goods: a small discrepancy in documents can allow the bank to refuse payment even if the goods are perfect.
items.example: A Ludhiana textile exporter sells fabric worth $80,000 to a buyer in Dubai. The buyer's bank in Dubai issues an irrevocable 60-day usance LC; an Indian bank advises it. The exporter ships, presents compliant documents and the Indian bank negotiates them. At ₹88 per dollar, the bill value is ₹70.4 lakh. If the Indian bank discounts the bill at 7% a year for 60 days, the exporter gets about 70.4 lakh × (1 − 0.07 × 60/365) = ₹69.59 lakh immediately.
faqs: What does 'banks deal in documents, not goods' mean?

Under UCP 600, the bank checks only whether the presented documents strictly comply with the LC's terms. It does not inspect the actual goods. If the documents comply, the bank must pay even if the buyer later finds a quality issue; if they don't, the bank can refuse even if the goods are fine.
What is a confirmed letter of credit?

A confirmed LC carries an additional undertaking from a second bank, usually in the exporter's country, to pay if documents comply. Exporters ask for confirmation when they doubt the issuing bank's strength or the buyer country's political or currency risk. The confirming bank charges a fee for taking on this risk.

items.title: Cash Credit vs Overdraft: Meaning, Drawing Power, Example
items.description: Cash credit and overdraft are running loan accounts charging interest only on the amount used. Learn drawing power, security, NPA rules and key differences.
items.short: Cash credit and overdraft are running loan accounts that let a borrower withdraw up to a sanctioned limit, paying interest only on the amount actually used and only for the days used.
body: Cash credit (CC) is the main working capital loan for traders and manufacturers. It is secured by hypothecation or pledge of current assets such as stock and receivables. The amount the borrower can actually draw at any time is the drawing power (DP), calculated from the latest stock statement: value of eligible stock and debtors minus the bank's margin. The borrower can draw the lower of the sanctioned limit and DP.

An overdraft (OD) lets a customer draw beyond the balance in a current or savings account. It may be secured against fixed deposits, property, shares or insurance policies, or be unsecured for salaried customers. OD limits are often fixed or reducing, and they are commonly used for short-term or personal needs rather than inventory financing.

Both accounts are reviewed periodically, usually once a year. For NPA classification, they are treated as 'out of order' if the outstanding balance remains continuously above the sanctioned limit or DP for 90 days, or if there are no credits for 90 days or credits are not enough to cover the interest debited. Drawing power based on stock statements older than three months is treated as irregular.

Key differences: CC is mainly for businesses and linked to current assets, while OD can be given to individuals and is linked to other security. Banks have also shifted large working capital borrowers partly to a loan component under RBI's 'loan system for delivery of bank credit' to improve fund planning.
items.example: A trader has a CC limit of ₹50 lakh. His stock is ₹40 lakh and eligible debtors ₹20 lakh. With a 25% margin on both, DP = (40 + 20) × 75% = ₹45 lakh, so he can draw at most ₹45 lakh, not ₹50 lakh. If he uses ₹30 lakh for 20 days at 10% a year, interest = 30,00,000 × 10% × 20/365 = about ₹16,438. Separately, his salaried brother takes an OD of ₹2 lakh against a ₹2.5 lakh FD.
faqs: What is drawing power in a cash credit account?

Drawing power is the maximum amount a borrower can actually withdraw at a given time, based on current assets like stock and receivables after deducting the bank's margin. It is updated from monthly or quarterly stock statements. Even if the sanctioned limit is higher, the borrower cannot draw beyond the drawing power.
When does a cash credit account become an NPA?

A CC or OD account becomes NPA when it stays 'out of order' for more than 90 days. That happens if the outstanding balance stays continuously above the sanctioned limit or drawing power, or if credits are absent or not enough to cover interest debited over the period. Old stock statements can also make DP irregular.

items.title: What is an NBFC? Meaning and Difference from a Bank
items.description: An NBFC lends and invests like a bank but cannot take demand deposits or issue cheques. Learn RBI registration, scale-based regulation and NBFC vs bank.
items.short: A non-banking financial company is a company registered under the Companies Act whose principal business is lending, investing, leasing or hire purchase, but which is not a bank.
body: NBFCs must register with RBI under Section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934, and hold minimum net owned funds as prescribed. The 'principal business' test applies: if financial assets are more than 50% of total assets and income from financial assets is more than 50% of gross income, the company is treated as an NBFC. Companies doing agriculture, industrial activity, trading in goods or buying property as their main business are not NBFCs.

Three key differences from banks: NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits (current and savings accounts); they are not part of the payment and settlement system and cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves; and deposits with deposit-taking NBFCs are not insured by DICGC. Only a small number of NBFCs are allowed to accept public fixed deposits, with limits on tenure and interest rates.

RBI introduced scale-based regulation in October 2022, dividing NBFCs into Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer and a Top Layer (kept empty unless needed). The bigger and more interconnected an NBFC, the stricter the rules, with Upper Layer NBFCs facing bank-like capital and governance requirements and mandatory listing. Types include investment and credit companies, housing finance companies, microfinance institutions, infrastructure finance companies and core investment companies.
Some financial firms are not regulated by RBI despite being finance companies: insurance companies (IRDAI), stock brokers and mutual funds (SEBI) and chit funds (state governments).
items.example: Rahul takes a ₹6 lakh two-wheeler and personal loan bundle from an NBFC at 14% while his bank offered 11.5% but needed more paperwork. His father considers a 3-year NBFC fixed deposit at 8.5% against 7% at a bank. On ₹5 lakh, the NBFC FD would earn about ₹1.39 lakh over three years (compounded annually) versus about ₹1.13 lakh at the bank. But the NBFC deposit has no DICGC cover, while the bank deposit is insured up to ₹5 lakh.
faqs: Can an NBFC open a savings account for customers?

No. NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits, which include savings and current accounts. Only some RBI-approved deposit-taking NBFCs can accept fixed deposits, for limited tenures. NBFCs also cannot issue cheque books on themselves because they are not part of the payment and settlement system.
Who regulates NBFCs in India?

Most NBFCs are registered and regulated by RBI under the RBI Act. Housing finance companies were moved from NHB to RBI regulation in 2019, though NHB still supervises them. Some finance-related entities are regulated by others: insurers by IRDAI, merchant bankers and mutual funds by SEBI, and chit funds by state governments.

items.title: Small Finance Bank (SFB): Meaning, Rules and Examples
items.description: Small finance banks are full banks focused on small borrowers and the unbanked. Learn RBI rules on capital, PSL, loan size, CRAR and how SFBs differ.
items.short: A small finance bank is a specialised bank licensed by RBI to accept deposits and lend, with a mandate to serve small businesses, small farmers, low-income households and the unorganised sector.
body: The concept came from the Nachiket Mor Committee (2014) on financial inclusion, and RBI issued SFB guidelines in November 2014. Ten entities got in-principle approval in 2015, many of them microfinance institutions such as Ujjivan, Equitas and Jana, along with AU Financiers, a vehicle finance NBFC. Since 2019 licences are 'on tap'.

SFBs are licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act and can do almost everything a commercial bank does: savings, current and fixed deposits, loans, debit and credit cards, and distribution of mutual funds and insurance. They must maintain CRR and SLR, and their deposits are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh.

Special conditions reflect their purpose. The minimum paid-up capital for new SFBs is ₹200 crore. At least 50% of their loan portfolio must be loans of up to ₹25 lakh. They have a much higher priority sector target than universal banks (75% of ANBC originally, later revised by RBI). Their minimum capital adequacy ratio is 15%. Promoters must hold at least 40% initially and reduce in phases. Check RBI's current guidelines for exact figures (as of 2026).

RBI allows well-run, listed SFBs meeting conditions on net worth, profitability and asset quality to apply to become universal banks, and AU Small Finance Bank received in-principle approval in 2025. A common confusion: an SFB is a full bank, unlike a payments bank, which cannot lend.
items.example: An SFB has a loan book of ₹20,000 crore. At least 50%, or ₹10,000 crore, must be in loans up to ₹25 lakh each, like microfinance loans of ₹50,000 and MSE loans of ₹10 lakh. With risk-weighted assets of ₹16,000 crore, it needs capital of at least 15% = ₹2,400 crore, compared with ₹1,840 crore at the 11.5% that applies to a universal bank. Its depositors enjoy the same ₹5 lakh DICGC cover as at any bank.
faqs: Is it safe to keep money in a small finance bank?

SFBs are scheduled banks regulated by RBI with the same CRR, SLR and supervision as other banks, and their deposits are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor. Like any bank, each SFB's financial health differs, so depositors can check capital adequacy and asset quality in published results.
What is the main difference between a small finance bank and a payments bank?

A small finance bank can both accept deposits and lend money, including to small businesses and farmers. A payments bank can accept deposits only up to ₹2 lakh per customer and cannot lend at all. SFBs are full-service niche banks; payments banks focus on payments and remittances.

items.title: Payments Bank Meaning: What It Can and Cannot Do
items.description: Payments banks accept small deposits and offer payments and remittances but cannot lend. Learn the ₹2 lakh deposit cap, investment rules and examples.
items.short: A payments bank is a differentiated bank licensed by RBI to accept small deposits and provide payments and remittance services, but which is not allowed to give loans.
body: Payments banks were also an idea of the Nachiket Mor Committee, meant to bring basic banking to migrant workers, low-income households and small businesses using technology and agent networks. RBI issued guidelines in November 2014 and gave in-principle approval to 11 applicants in 2015. Operational examples include Airtel Payments Bank, India Post Payments Bank, Fino Payments Bank, Jio Payments Bank and NSDL Payments Bank.

Permitted activities: savings and current accounts with a maximum end-of-day balance of ₹2 lakh per customer (raised from ₹1 lakh in 2021); debit cards and ATM cards; payments and remittances through UPI, IMPS, NEFT and AePS; bill payments; and distribution of mutual funds, insurance and pension products. They can act as business correspondents of other banks. Not permitted: any lending, credit cards, or accepting NRI deposits.

Because they cannot lend, payments banks must hold at least 75% of demand deposit balances in SLR-eligible government securities and treasury bills of up to one year maturity, and can keep at most 25% in current and time deposits with other scheduled banks. Their minimum paid-up capital is ₹100 crore, and capital adequacy is set at 15%. Earnings come from fees, float income and distribution.

Payments banks are regulated like other banks on KYC and compliance. In 2024 RBI barred Paytm Payments Bank from accepting fresh deposits over persistent non-compliance, a reminder that regulatory obligations apply in full.
items.example: A worker in Surat keeps his wages in a payments bank account linked to UPI. At the end of a day his balance reaches ₹2.3 lakh after a bonus. Since the limit is ₹2 lakh, the excess ₹30,000 is swept automatically into a partner bank's account if he has opted for that facility. Of the payments bank's ₹1,000 crore demand deposits, at least ₹750 crore must be in government securities or T-bills of up to one year.
faqs: Can a payments bank give loans?

No. Payments banks are prohibited from lending in any form, including credit cards. They can, however, distribute loan products of other banks or NBFCs as an agent, with the partner taking the credit risk. This restriction is the defining feature that separates them from small finance banks and universal banks.
Are deposits in a payments bank insured?

Yes. Payments banks are banks under the Banking Regulation Act, and their deposits are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor. Since the deposit limit itself is ₹2 lakh per customer, a depositor's balance in a payments bank will normally be fully covered.

items.title: Regional Rural Bank (RRB): Meaning, Ownership, History
items.description: RRBs are government-sponsored banks serving rural India. Learn the RRB Act 1976, the 50:35:15 ownership, NABARD's role and the merger drive in this guide.
items.short: Regional Rural Banks are scheduled commercial banks set up to provide credit and banking services in rural areas, especially to small farmers, labourers, artisans and small entrepreneurs.
body: RRBs were created following the Narasimham Working Group (1975). The first five RRBs began on 2 October 1975 under an ordinance, the earliest being Prathama Bank in Moradabad, sponsored by Syndicate Bank. The Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976 then gave them a legal framework. The aim was to combine the local feel of co-operatives with the professional management of commercial banks.

Ownership is shared: the Central Government holds 50%, the sponsor bank (a public or private sector bank) 35%, and the state government 15%. A 2015 amendment allowed RRBs to raise capital from the public, reducing the combined Centre and sponsor stake to not less than 51%. The sponsor bank provides management support, staff and refinance.

RRBs are regulated by RBI and supervised by NABARD. Their priority sector lending target is 75% of ANBC, much higher than commercial banks. They are scheduled commercial banks but are not allowed to access some RBI facilities like LAF in the same way.

RRB numbers have fallen sharply through amalgamation, from 196 at their peak to 43 by 2021 and fewer after the 'One State, One RRB' consolidation in 2025. Check NABARD or the Finance Ministry for the current number (as of 2026). IBPS conducts a separate RRB recruitment exam for Officer Scale and Office Assistant posts.
items.example: A new RRB is set up with authorised capital raised in the standard ratio. If its issued capital is ₹200 crore, the Centre contributes 50% = ₹100 crore, the sponsor bank 35% = ₹70 crore, and the state government 15% = ₹30 crore. If its ANBC is ₹6,000 crore, its PSL requirement at 75% is ₹4,500 crore, compared with ₹2,400 crore at 40% for a commercial bank of the same size.
faqs: Who owns Regional Rural Banks?

RRBs are jointly owned by the Central Government (50%), the sponsor bank (35%) and the concerned state government (15%). The 2015 amendment to the RRB Act allows them to raise capital from other sources, provided the Centre and sponsor bank together keep at least 51%. Most sponsor banks are public sector banks.
Which body supervises RRBs?

RBI is the regulator for RRBs, but on-site supervision and inspection are carried out by NABARD under powers delegated by RBI. NABARD also provides refinance to RRBs for agriculture and rural lending. This dual arrangement is a frequent question in banking exams.

items.title: RBI Ombudsman Scheme: How to Complain About a Bank
