items.description: The RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021 handles complaints against banks, NBFCs and payment firms for free. Learn eligibility, timelines and compensation.
items.short: The RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme is a free grievance redressal system under which customers can complain against banks, NBFCs and payment system participants for deficiency in service.
body: Launched on 12 November 2021, the scheme merged three earlier schemes, the Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006, the NBFC Ombudsman Scheme 2018 and the Digital Transactions Ombudsman Scheme 2019, under a 'One Nation, One Ombudsman' approach. Complaints can be filed online on RBI's Complaint Management System portal, by email or by post to the Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre at RBI Chandigarh, and help is available on toll-free number 14448.

It covers commercial banks, regional rural banks, scheduled primary urban co-operative banks and larger non-scheduled ones, eligible NBFCs, prepaid payment instrument issuers, payment system participants and credit information companies. Any 'deficiency in service', such as failure to credit a transfer, unauthorised debits, unfair charges or delays, is a valid ground, rather than a fixed list as in older schemes.

Conditions: the customer must first complain to the regulated entity. If it rejects the complaint, gives an unsatisfactory reply or does not reply within 30 days, the customer may approach the Ombudsman within one year of the reply (or one year and 30 days from the complaint if no reply). Complaints already pending in a court or other forum are not entertained. There is no fee.

The Ombudsman first tries conciliation. If that fails, it can pass an award of up to ₹20 lakh for consequential loss plus up to ₹1 lakh for loss of time, expenses, harassment and mental anguish. Either party may appeal to the Appellate Authority, an Executive Director of RBI, within 30 days. Figures are as of 2026; check RBI.
items.example: On 3 March, ₹18,000 is debited from Meera's account for a failed ATM withdrawal. She complains to her bank the same day. RBI's turnaround rules require auto-reversal within five working days, with ₹100 per day compensation for delay. The bank does not respond by 2 April (30 days), so she files on the RBI CMS portal. The Ombudsman directs the bank to refund ₹18,000 and pay the delay compensation, without Meera paying any fee.
faqs: Can I go to the RBI Ombudsman directly without complaining to my bank?

No. You must first complain in writing to the bank or other regulated entity. You can approach the Ombudsman only if the entity rejects the complaint, you are not satisfied with the reply, or it does not reply within 30 days. Keep the complaint reference number as proof.
Is there any fee to file a complaint with the RBI Ombudsman?

No. The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme is completely free for customers. You can file online through the CMS portal, by email or by post without a lawyer. The regulated entity also cannot charge you for complaints. The Ombudsman's award is binding on the entity if you accept it.

items.title: Insurance Premium Meaning: How Premium Is Calculated
items.description: An insurance premium is the price paid for cover. Learn how insurers set premium using mortality, interest and expenses, payment modes and what raises it.
items.short: An insurance premium is the amount a policyholder pays the insurer, once or at regular intervals, in exchange for the insurer's promise to pay benefits on the insured event.
body: Premium is the consideration that makes an insurance contract valid. In life insurance, it is built from three elements. The risk premium covers the expected cost of claims, based on mortality tables (Indian insurers use the Indian Assured Lives Mortality table). Interest is credited because premiums are collected in advance and invested. Loading is added for the insurer's expenses, commissions, contingencies and profit. The result is the office premium, the amount the customer actually pays.

Factors that raise a life premium: higher age at entry, larger sum assured, longer term, smoking or tobacco use, health conditions, hazardous occupations and adverse family history. In general insurance, premium depends on the value and risk of the subject matter: for motor, the vehicle's insured declared value, cubic capacity and claim history; for health, age, city, sum insured and plan features.

Payment modes include single premium, yearly, half-yearly, quarterly and monthly. Yearly payment is cheapest overall because insurers charge a modal loading for more frequent payments, and some give a rebate for large sum assured. Level premium means the same premium every year even though risk rises with age; the excess paid in early years builds a reserve that funds later years.

Exam pointers: premium in advance is a basic principle under Section 64VB of the Insurance Act for general insurance, where cover starts only after premium is received. Indirect tax on premium depends on product type; individual life and health policies were exempted from GST from September 2025. Premium paid is not refundable once risk has run, except as policy terms allow.
items.example: Two 30-year-olds buy a ₹1 crore, 30-year term plan. The non-smoker pays an annual premium of, say, ₹12,000; the smoker pays ₹19,500, about 62% more, for the same cover. If the non-smoker chooses monthly payments of ₹1,050, the yearly total becomes ₹12,600, which is ₹600 (5%) more than paying annually, because of the modal loading. Over 30 years, that small difference adds up to ₹18,000.
faqs: Why is the premium for smokers higher?

Smokers and tobacco users have statistically higher mortality and illness rates, so the expected cost of claims is higher. Insurers price this extra risk through higher rates. Concealing tobacco use to get a lower premium is a breach of utmost good faith and can lead to claim rejection within the period allowed under Section 45.
Is GST charged on life insurance premium?

From 22 September 2025 the GST Council exempted premiums on individual life and individual health insurance policies, including term plans. Group policies and most general insurance, such as motor and fire, still attract GST. Rates and exemptions are set by the GST Council and can change, so check the current position (as of 2026).

items.title: Sum Assured Meaning in Life Insurance with Example
items.description: Sum assured is the guaranteed amount a life insurer pays on death or maturity. Learn sum assured vs sum insured, how to choose it and the HLV method.
items.short: Sum assured is the fixed amount of money that a life insurance company promises to pay on the occurrence of the insured event, such as death of the life assured or maturity of the policy.
body: In a term plan, sum assured is the death benefit paid to the nominee. In an endowment plan, it is typically payable on death during the term or on survival to maturity, along with any bonuses declared. Some plans pay a higher 'sum assured on death', defined by IRDAI rules as the highest of a multiple of annual premium, the basic sum assured, or a percentage of premiums paid.

Sum assured differs from sum insured. Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity because a human life cannot be valued exactly, so the insurer pays a fixed, agreed amount. General insurance like health, motor and fire is indemnity-based: the 'sum insured' is the maximum the insurer will pay, and the actual claim is limited to the real loss.

How much to choose? A common method is Human Life Value (HLV), which estimates the present value of the income a person's family would lose. A simpler rule of thumb is a multiple of annual income, often 10 to 15 times, adjusted for loans and goals. Insurers also apply financial underwriting: they will not issue a sum assured far beyond what the person's income justifies, to avoid over-insurance and moral hazard.

Riders have their own sum assured, usually not more than the base policy. Exam pointer: premium is directly proportional to sum assured for the same age and term, so a ₹50 lakh cover costs roughly half of a ₹1 crore cover, though rebates for larger covers can make the larger one slightly cheaper per lakh.
items.example: Amit, 32, earns ₹9 lakh a year; about ₹2.5 lakh goes on his own expenses and taxes, so his family relies on ₹6.5 lakh a year. Assuming 28 working years left and a 6% discount rate, the present value is about ₹6.5 lakh × 13.41 = ₹87 lakh. He also has a ₹25 lakh home loan, so he might consider a term cover of around ₹1.1 to 1.2 crore. If he dies during the term, his nominee receives the sum assured.
faqs: What is the difference between sum assured and sum insured?

Sum assured is used in life insurance and is the fixed amount paid on death or maturity, regardless of actual financial loss. Sum insured is used in general insurance such as health, motor and property, and is the maximum limit; the claim paid is the actual loss up to that limit, following the principle of indemnity.
Can I get a sum assured of any amount I want?

No. Insurers use financial underwriting to check that the sum assured is reasonable compared with your income, age and existing cover. They may ask for income proof for larger amounts. Very high cover relative to income may be declined or reduced because it could create a motive for fraud.

items.title: Insurance Riders Meaning: Types, Limits and Example
items.description: Riders are optional add-ons to a base insurance policy for extra cover. Learn accidental death, critical illness and premium waiver riders with an example.
items.short: A rider is an optional add-on benefit attached to a base insurance policy, for an extra premium, that provides cover beyond what the main policy offers.
body: Riders cannot be bought alone; they ride on a base policy. Common life insurance riders include: Accidental Death Benefit (ADB), paying an extra sum if death is due to an accident; Accidental Total and Permanent Disability, paying if an accident leaves the insured unable to work; Critical Illness, paying a lump sum on diagnosis of listed illnesses like cancer, heart attack or stroke; Waiver of Premium, under which future premiums are waived if the policyholder dies or becomes disabled; Term rider, adding extra life cover; and Hospital Cash.

Riders are cheaper than buying separate policies because the insurer saves on administration and underwriting. But they end when the base policy ends or lapses, and their benefits are usually more limited than standalone covers. IRDAI rules cap rider benefits and premiums: the rider sum assured generally cannot exceed the base sum assured, and there are limits on rider premium as a share of the base premium. Check IRDAI product regulations for current limits (as of 2026).

Under IRDAI rules, rider terms must be disclosed clearly and the policyholder can generally add or remove certain riders at policy anniversaries, depending on product terms. Rider claims are assessed separately: an accidental death claim requires proof that death was caused by an accident, not illness.

A frequent misunderstanding: a waiver of premium rider does not pay money to the family; it keeps the policy going by paying future premiums. Another is assuming an ADB rider covers death from any cause; it covers only accidental death within a time window after the accident.
items.example: Sanjay buys a ₹50 lakh term plan with a ₹25 lakh ADB rider and a ₹10 lakh critical illness rider. If he is diagnosed with a listed cancer in year 5, the CI rider pays ₹10 lakh and the term cover continues. If he later dies in a road accident, the nominee gets ₹50 lakh + ₹25 lakh = ₹75 lakh. If he died of an illness instead, the nominee would get only the base ₹50 lakh.
faqs: Can a rider be bought without a base policy?

No. A rider is an add-on that can only be attached to a base life or health insurance policy. If you want standalone protection, you can buy a separate personal accident or critical illness policy instead. When the base policy lapses, matures or is surrendered, the attached riders also end.
What is a waiver of premium rider?

It is a rider under which the insurer pays all future premiums of the base policy if the policyholder dies or suffers a specified disability or critical illness, depending on the variant. It is common in child plans where the parent is the proposer, so the child's policy continues even if the parent is no longer there.

items.title: Free-Look Period in Insurance: Meaning and Refund Rules
items.description: The free-look period lets a policyholder return a new insurance policy and get a refund if unhappy with its terms. Learn the duration, deductions and example.
items.short: The free-look period is a window after receiving a new insurance policy during which the policyholder can review it and return it for a refund if not satisfied with the terms.
body: IRDAI introduced the free-look provision to protect buyers from mis-selling. Once you receive the policy document, you can read the terms, exclusions and charges, and if they are not what you were told, cancel without penalty, stating your reasons. Under the IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) Regulations and the 2024 master circular, the free-look period for life and health policies is 30 days from the receipt of the policy document, whether physical or electronic. Earlier it was 15 days, with 30 days for distance marketing. Check IRDAI for current rules (as of 2026).

The refund is not always the full premium. For traditional life policies, the insurer may deduct proportionate risk premium for the days of cover, the cost of medical examination and stamp duty. For ULIPs, the insurer also adjusts for the change in unit value, so the refund equals the fund value on cancellation plus non-allocated premium and charges levied, minus the permitted deductions.

The free-look option is not available for policies with tenure of less than one year in some categories, such as short-term travel or motor insurance, and normally applies to new policies, not renewals. In health insurance, it also does not apply to portability renewals in the same way.
Common confusion: free-look is different from the grace period. Free-look is at the start of a policy to cancel it; grace period is the time allowed to pay a renewal premium after the due date.
items.example: Deepa buys a traditional life policy with an annual premium of ₹48,000. She receives the policy document on 1 June and finds charges she wasn't told about. On 20 June she submits a free-look cancellation. The insurer deducts proportionate risk premium for 20 days (say ₹180), medical tests of ₹1,500 and stamp duty of ₹200. Refund = 48,000 − 180 − 1,500 − 200 = ₹46,120.
faqs: Will I get my full premium back in the free-look period?

Not always. The insurer may deduct the proportionate risk premium for the days you were covered, stamp duty, and medical examination costs. For ULIPs, the refund is also adjusted for any change in the value of the units. Still, the deductions are small compared with surrendering a policy later.
When does the free-look period start?

It starts from the date you receive the policy document, not from the date of payment or issuance. For electronic policies, it is the date of receipt of the electronic document. Keeping proof of the delivery date, such as a courier receipt or email timestamp, helps if there is a dispute.

items.title: Grace Period in Insurance: Meaning, Days and Rules
items.description: The grace period is extra time after the premium due date during which a policy stays in force. Learn 30-day and 15-day rules, claims in grace, and lapse.
items.short: The grace period is a fixed number of days after the premium due date within which the policyholder can pay the premium without the policy lapsing and without losing benefits.
body: In life insurance, the standard grace period is 30 days for yearly, half-yearly and quarterly modes, and 15 days for monthly mode, as set out in IRDAI product regulations. During the grace period the policy remains fully in force. If the life assured dies within the grace period before paying, the insurer pays the claim after deducting the unpaid premium.

If the premium is not paid by the end of the grace period, a traditional policy lapses (or becomes paid-up if it has acquired a paid-up value), and a ULIP moves to the discontinued policy fund if it is within the lock-in. Most insurers do not charge interest for payment within the grace period, though they may add late fees after it.

In health insurance, the grace period for renewal is typically 30 days (some insurers allow more for monthly or instalment payment), and continuity benefits such as waiting periods already served are preserved if premium is paid within it. However, health insurers usually do not cover illnesses or hospitalisation that occur during the grace period before renewal premium is paid, so the policy is continuous but cover for that gap may be excluded. Read the policy wording. Check IRDAI rules for current durations (as of 2026).
Exam traps: grace period does not apply to single premium policies; and it is not the same as the free-look period or the revival period.
items.example: Ravi's quarterly premium of ₹6,000 on a life policy with sum assured ₹10 lakh is due on 1 March. The grace period runs 30 days, till 31 March. He dies in an accident on 20 March without having paid. The insurer pays the death claim of ₹10 lakh minus the unpaid ₹6,000, so the nominee receives ₹9,94,000. Had he died on 5 April with premium still unpaid, the policy would have lapsed and the claim could be rejected.
faqs: Is my life insured during the grace period?

Yes. During the grace period the life policy is in force with full cover. If a claim arises, the insurer settles it after deducting the premium that was due. Once the grace period expires without payment, the policy lapses or becomes paid-up, depending on how many premiums have been paid.
What is the grace period for a monthly premium policy?

For life insurance policies with monthly premium payment, the grace period is 15 days. For yearly, half-yearly and quarterly modes it is 30 days. These durations come from IRDAI product regulations; individual policies may offer more, so check the policy document.

items.title: Lapsed Policy Revival: Meaning, Period and Process
items.description: A policy lapses when premium is not paid within the grace period. Learn what lapse means, the revival period, revival charges and how revival works.
items.short: A policy lapses when the premium is not paid by the end of the grace period, ending the insurance cover; revival is the process of restoring it by paying arrears and meeting conditions.
body: When a policy lapses, the insurer is no longer liable to pay the death benefit. For traditional policies, if premiums were paid for the minimum period needed to acquire a paid-up value (usually set in the product terms), the policy does not fully lapse but becomes 'paid-up' with a reduced sum assured. For ULIPs within the five-year lock-in, the fund moves to a discontinued policy fund.

Revival lets the policyholder restore full benefits within a revival period. IRDAI product regulations allow five years from the date of the first unpaid premium for non-linked policies and three years for linked policies (ULIPs). Check the latest IRDAI rules (as of 2026). To revive, the policyholder must pay all overdue premiums with interest at the rate set by the insurer, and submit a declaration of good health; for longer lapses or large covers, the insurer may require a fresh medical examination.

The insurer can accept, reject or accept the revival with modified terms, because the risk may have changed since the policy was issued. Once revived, the contestability period under Section 45 restarts from the date of revival for statements made at revival. Some insurers run special revival campaigns with reduced late fees.

Common misunderstanding: reviving an old policy is often cheaper than buying a new one at an older age, but it is not automatic. Also, any claim during the lapsed period is not covered, even if the policy is later revived.
items.example: Ramesh's annual premium of ₹24,000 fell due on 1 June 2024 and he did not pay it then, nor on 1 June 2025. In August 2025 he wants to revive. Arrears = ₹48,000. If the insurer charges 9% simple interest, interest ≈ 24,000 × 9% × 14.5/12 + 24,000 × 9% × 2.5/12 = ₹2,610 + ₹450 = ₹3,060. He pays about ₹51,060 and submits a good-health declaration. He is within five years from the first unpaid premium, so revival is allowed.
faqs: Can a lapsed policy always be revived?

Only within the revival period, which is five years for traditional and three years for unit-linked policies under IRDAI rules, and subject to the insurer's acceptance of risk. The insurer can ask for medical tests and may refuse or impose conditions if health has worsened. After the revival period, the policy cannot be revived.
What happens to the money paid in a lapsed policy?

It depends on how long premiums were paid. If the policy acquired a surrender or paid-up value, you can receive the surrender value or keep a reduced paid-up cover. If it lapsed very early, before acquiring any value, the premiums paid may be lost, which is why early lapse is costly.

items.title: Surrender Value in Life Insurance: GSV vs SSV Explained
items.description: Surrender value is the amount an insurer pays if you exit a life policy before maturity. Learn guaranteed vs special surrender value with a worked example.
items.short: Surrender value is the amount a life insurer pays the policyholder who voluntarily ends the policy before maturity, after it has acquired a surrender value under its terms.
body: When you surrender a policy, the contract ends and all future benefits, including life cover, stop. You receive the surrender value, which is usually well below the premiums paid in the early years because the insurer has already spent on commissions, underwriting and the risk cover provided.

Traditional policies quote two values. The Guaranteed Surrender Value (GSV) is a minimum stated in the policy, calculated as a percentage of total premiums paid (excluding extra premiums and rider premiums), with the percentage rising with the number of years the policy has run. The Special Surrender Value (SSV) is a non-guaranteed amount the insurer calculates using the paid-up value, accrued bonuses and a surrender factor; it is often higher than the GSV. The insurer pays the higher of the two.

When does a policy acquire surrender value? Older rules required at least two or three full years' premiums. IRDAI's 2024 product regulations allow surrender value after one full year's premium in many cases and require insurers to make early-exit values fairer. Check the product brochure and current IRDAI rules (as of 2026). For ULIPs, surrender within the five-year lock-in moves the money to a discontinued policy fund, paid out only after the lock-in ends, minus a capped discontinuance charge.

A common mistake is surrendering a long-term policy in a hurry for cash. Alternatives include a policy loan (up to a percentage of surrender value), making it paid-up, or assigning it. Surrender can also have tax consequences, so check before acting.
items.example: Kavita paid ₹30,000 a year for 5 years on a 20-year endowment plan, total ₹1,50,000. The GSV factor for year 5 is, say, 50%, so GSV = ₹75,000. Her paid-up sum assured is ₹6 lakh × 5/20 = ₹1,50,000; with ₹40,000 of bonuses, total paid-up value = ₹1,90,000. With an SSV factor of 0.48, SSV = ₹91,200. She receives the higher value, ₹91,200, and her ₹6 lakh life cover ends.
faqs: Why is surrender value so low in the early years?

In the first few years, a large part of the premium goes towards agent commission, policy issue costs, underwriting and the cost of life cover already provided. Only the remaining part is invested for the policyholder. Surrender values are therefore low early on and improve as the policy runs longer.
Is surrendering better than letting a policy lapse?

If the policy has acquired a surrender value, surrendering returns some money, while lapsing may convert it to a reduced paid-up policy that still provides some cover and pays at maturity. The better choice depends on your need for cover and cash. A policy loan is another option if the need for money is temporary.

items.title: Nomination in Life Insurance: Section 39 Rules Explained
items.description: Nomination names who receives a life policy's money on the insured's death. Learn Section 39 rules, beneficial nominees, appointee for minors and changes.
items.short: Nomination is the policyholder's choice of the person or persons who should receive the policy money if the life assured dies, governed by Section 39 of the Insurance Act, 1938.
body: Only the holder of a policy on his own life can nominate. Nomination can be made at the time of buying the policy or later, by an endorsement on the policy or a written notice to the insurer, and it can be changed any number of times during the policy term. Multiple nominees can be named, with shares specified.

Before 2015, a nominee was only a trustee who received the money on behalf of the legal heirs. The Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015 introduced 'beneficial nominees': if the nominee is the policyholder's parent, spouse, children, or spouse and children, the nominee is entitled to the money in their own right. For other nominees, such as a brother or friend, the old position still applies and the legal heirs can claim the money.

If the nominee is a minor, the policyholder must appoint an appointee, an adult who receives the money on the minor's behalf until the minor turns 18. If the nominee dies before the policyholder, the nomination fails, and without a new nomination the money goes to the policyholder's legal heirs, which can mean succession certificates and delay.

Nomination and assignment interact: an assignment (other than to the insurer for a policy loan) cancels the nomination automatically. Under the Married Women's Property Act policies (Section 6), nomination is not permitted because the policy already creates a trust for the wife and children.
items.example: Vikas takes a ₹75 lakh term plan and nominates his wife 60% and his 12-year-old son 40%, naming his mother as appointee. If he dies, his wife receives ₹45 lakh as a beneficial nominee. His son's share of ₹30 lakh is paid to the appointee, his mother, who holds it for the son until he turns 18. If Vikas had nominated his brother instead, the brother would receive ₹75 lakh only as a trustee for the legal heirs.
faqs: What is a beneficial nominee?

Introduced by the 2015 amendment to Section 39, a beneficial nominee is a parent, spouse or child of the policyholder named as nominee. Such a nominee receives the policy money as their own, and legal heirs cannot claim it. Any other nominee only receives the money as a trustee for the legal heirs.
Can I change my nominee after buying a policy?

Yes. You can change or cancel a nomination any number of times during the policy term by submitting a written request or endorsement to the insurer. The insurer records the change and acknowledges it. Payment made to the last registered nominee in good faith discharges the insurer's liability.

items.title: Assignment of Life Insurance Policy: Section 38 Meaning
items.description: Assignment transfers the rights in a life policy to another person or bank. Learn absolute vs conditional assignment, Section 38 and the nomination effect.
items.short: Assignment is the legal transfer of the rights, title and interest in a life insurance policy from the policyholder (assignor) to another person or institution (assignee), under Section 38 of the Insurance Act.
body: Assignment is usually done when a policy is used as security for a loan, or to gift the benefits to someone. It can be done by an endorsement on the policy or by a separate instrument, signed by the assignor and attested by at least one witness, and it must state the fact of transfer and reasons. The assignment takes effect against the insurer only when written notice is given to the insurer, which then registers it.

Types: an absolute assignment transfers all rights permanently to the assignee, who can then surrender the policy, take a loan or receive claims. A conditional assignment transfers rights subject to a condition, typically that the rights revert to the assignor if he survives to maturity, or that the policy is reassigned when a loan is repaid. Banks commonly take conditional assignment of policies as collateral for home loans.

Key points from the 2015 amendment: the insurer may decline to act on an assignment if it believes it is not bona fide, not in the policyholder's interest, or for trafficking in policies, giving reasons in writing; the decision can be appealed to IRDAI within 30 days. An assignment automatically cancels an existing nomination, except an assignment to the insurer itself for a policy loan.
Difference from nomination: nomination only decides who receives money on death and gives no rights during the policyholder's lifetime; assignment transfers ownership of the rights immediately.
items.example: Neha takes a ₹40 lakh home loan and conditionally assigns her ₹50 lakh term policy to the bank. The bank registers the assignment with the insurer, and her earlier nomination of her husband is cancelled. If she dies with ₹32 lakh of loan outstanding, the insurer pays ₹50 lakh: ₹32 lakh to the bank and, after reassignment, the remaining ₹18 lakh as per her estate or fresh nomination. Once she repays the loan, the bank reassigns the policy and she can nominate again.
faqs: What happens to nomination when a policy is assigned?

Under Section 39(7) of the Insurance Act, an assignment automatically cancels any existing nomination. The exception is an assignment to the insurer itself as security for a policy loan, in which case the nomination is affected only to the extent of the insurer's interest. After reassignment, the policyholder should make a fresh nomination.
Can an insurer refuse to register an assignment?

Yes, since the 2015 amendment the insurer may refuse if it has sufficient reason to believe the assignment is not bona fide, not in the policyholder's interest, against public policy, or meant for trading in policies. It must record its reasons in writing, and the policyholder can appeal to IRDAI within 30 days.

items.title: Insurable Interest Meaning in Insurance with Examples
items.description: Insurable interest means you suffer a financial loss if the insured life or property is harmed. Learn when it must exist in life, fire and marine insurance.
items.short: Insurable interest is the legally recognised financial interest a person has in the life or property being insured, such that its loss or damage would cause that person a financial loss.
body: Insurable interest is what separates insurance from a bet. Without it, anyone could insure a stranger's house or life and profit from its loss, which would be gambling and create a motive for harm. Every valid insurance contract needs it, along with the subject matter of insurance and premium as consideration.

In life insurance, a person has unlimited insurable interest in their own life. A husband and wife have insurable interest in each other's lives. For other relatives, such as parent and child or siblings, the law looks for a financial dependence or pecuniary interest rather than mere relationship, though insurers routinely allow a parent to propose a policy on a minor child's life. A creditor has insurable interest in a debtor's life up to the debt, an employer in a key employee's life (keyman insurance), and partners in each other's lives.

Timing differs by type. In life insurance, insurable interest must exist at the time of taking the policy; it need not exist at the time of claim. So a divorced spouse's policy remains valid. In fire and most property insurance, it must exist both at inception and at the time of loss. In marine insurance, it must exist at the time of loss, because cargo changes hands during the voyage.
Common confusion: insurable interest is about financial loss, not emotional attachment. A friend may be very close, but without a financial stake he cannot insure your life.
items.example: Arjun, a trader, sells goods worth ₹8 lakh on credit to Bimal and takes a policy on Bimal's life for ₹8 lakh, since Bimal's death could mean losing the debt. This is valid. He cannot insure Bimal for ₹50 lakh, as his interest is only ₹8 lakh. Separately, Arjun's warehouse with stock worth ₹30 lakh is insured for fire; if he sells the warehouse in June and a fire occurs in July, he cannot claim because he no longer has insurable interest at the time of loss.
faqs: When must insurable interest exist in life insurance?

In life insurance, insurable interest must exist at the time the policy is taken. It does not have to exist at the time of the claim. For example, if a wife insures her husband and they later divorce, the policy remains valid and the claim is payable if the insured event occurs.
Does a person have insurable interest in a friend's life?

Generally no, because a friend's death does not cause a recognised financial loss. Emotional closeness is not enough. However, if the friend owes money or is a business partner, there can be insurable interest limited to the financial stake, such as the debt amount or partnership interest.

items.title: Utmost Good Faith in Insurance: Uberrimae Fidei Explained
items.description: Utmost good faith requires both insurer and insured to disclose all material facts honestly. Learn material facts, non-disclosure effects and an example.
items.short: Utmost good faith, or uberrimae fidei, is the principle that both parties to an insurance contract must voluntarily disclose all material facts fully and accurately, whether asked or not.
body: Ordinary commercial contracts follow 'caveat emptor' (let the buyer beware), where each side looks after itself. Insurance is different because the proposer knows far more about the risk than the insurer: their health, habits, past illnesses, or the condition of their property. So the law imposes a higher duty of disclosure on both sides.

A material fact is any fact that would influence a prudent insurer's decision to accept the risk or fix the premium. Examples: age, existing diseases, past surgeries, smoking and alcohol habits, hazardous occupation, existing insurance policies, and for property, the nature of construction and goods stored. Facts that reduce risk, facts the insurer already knows, and matters of common knowledge need not be disclosed.

Breach can be non-disclosure (silence about a material fact), misrepresentation (an inaccurate statement), or concealment (deliberate hiding). The insurer may avoid the contract if the breach is material. However, under Section 45 of the Insurance Act, a life policy cannot be questioned on any ground after three years from issue or revival, which limits how long this defence is available.

The duty applies to the insurer too: it must explain policy terms, exclusions and charges clearly and not hide important conditions. The duty is strongest at proposal stage and continues at renewal and revival.
items.example: Ramesh, 42, applies for a ₹1 crore term plan and does not disclose that he has been on diabetes medication for four years. The insurer issues the policy at a standard premium of ₹22,000. He dies of a cardiac event 18 months later. During claim investigation, hospital records show the diabetes history. Because this was a material non-disclosure within three years, the insurer can repudiate the claim under Section 45, giving written reasons. Disclosure might have meant a loaded premium, perhaps ₹30,000, but a valid policy.
faqs: What is a material fact in insurance?

A material fact is any information that would influence an insurer's decision on whether to accept a risk, on what terms, or at what premium. Examples include pre-existing illnesses, smoking, risky occupations and previous claim history. If in doubt, the safer course is to disclose, because non-disclosure can lead to claim rejection.
Does utmost good faith apply to the insurer as well?

Yes. The insurer must also act in utmost good faith by disclosing policy terms, exclusions, charges and benefits clearly, and must not mislead the proposer. IRDAI's policyholder protection regulations require insurers to provide key information documents and explain features before sale.

items.title: Principle of Indemnity in Insurance: Meaning and Example
items.description: Indemnity means the insured is restored to the same financial position as before a loss, not better. Learn where it applies, its corollaries and an example.
items.short: The principle of indemnity says an insurance claim should restore the insured to the same financial position they were in just before the loss, no better and no worse.
body: Indemnity prevents people from profiting from insurance. If you could earn more from a claim than your actual loss, you might be tempted to cause or exaggerate losses. So general insurance such as fire, marine, motor, property and most health policies (hospitalisation reimbursement) pays only the actual loss, subject to the sum insured, deductibles and policy terms.

Indemnity can be provided in four ways: cash payment, repair, replacement, or reinstatement (restoring a building to its earlier condition). Actual loss in property insurance is usually the market value at the time of loss, which accounts for depreciation, unless the policy is on a reinstatement value or 'new for old' basis.

Two related principles flow from indemnity. Subrogation transfers the insured's rights against a third party to the insurer after it pays the claim, so the insured cannot recover twice. Contribution applies when the same property is insured with more than one insurer: each insurer shares the loss in proportion, and the insured cannot collect the full loss from each. Under-insurance triggers the 'average' clause: if the sum insured is less than the value, the claim is reduced proportionately.

Indemnity does not apply to life insurance or personal accident benefits (for death or disability), because a human life has no market value. These are 'benefit' or 'valued' policies that pay a fixed amount.
items.example: A shop's stock is worth ₹20 lakh but insured for only ₹15 lakh. A fire destroys stock worth ₹8 lakh. Under the average clause, the claim = 8 lakh × 15/20 = ₹6 lakh. If the stock had been fully insured for ₹20 lakh, the claim would be ₹8 lakh, the actual loss, not the ₹20 lakh sum insured. And if the owner also had a ₹10 lakh policy with another insurer, contribution would split the payout between them.
faqs: Why does indemnity not apply to life insurance?

Indemnity requires measuring the actual financial loss, but a human life cannot be valued precisely in money. So life insurance pays the agreed sum assured on death or maturity, regardless of the actual loss. That is why life policies are called benefit policies, while general insurance policies are contracts of indemnity.
What is the average clause in fire insurance?

If property is under-insured, meaning the sum insured is less than its actual value, the average clause reduces the claim in the same proportion. Claim = Loss × Sum insured ÷ Value of property. It encourages people to insure for full value and is a direct application of indemnity and fairness among policyholders.

items.title: Subrogation in Insurance: Meaning with a Simple Example
items.description: Subrogation lets an insurer, after paying a claim, recover the loss from the third party who caused it. Learn how it works, where it applies and an example.
items.short: Subrogation is the right of an insurer, after paying a claim, to step into the shoes of the insured and recover the amount from the third party responsible for the loss.
body: Subrogation is a corollary of the principle of indemnity. If an insured could collect from the insurer and also sue the person who caused the damage, they would recover twice and profit from the loss. Subrogation prevents this by transferring the insured's legal rights against the wrongdoer to the insurer, up to the amount the insurer has paid.

The insurer's right arises only after it has paid the claim. It can then sue in the insured's name or its own, and the insured must cooperate, for example by providing documents and evidence. If the insurer recovers more than it paid, the excess goes to the insured. Policies usually contain a subrogation clause, and the insured signs a letter of subrogation when receiving the claim.

The insured must not do anything that harms the insurer's subrogation rights, such as releasing the wrongdoer from liability or settling privately for a small sum. Doing so can reduce or void the claim. Insurers may also acquire salvage, the damaged property itself, which is a related form of recovery.

Subrogation applies to indemnity contracts such as motor, fire, marine and property insurance. It does not apply to life insurance or personal accident death benefits, which pay a fixed amount; the family can both receive the sum assured and sue the person responsible for the death.
items.example: Neeta's car, insured for an IDV of ₹6 lakh, is hit by a truck whose driver is at fault. Repairs cost ₹1,20,000. Her insurer pays ₹1,15,000 after the ₹5,000 compulsory deductible. Through subrogation, the insurer files a recovery claim against the truck owner's insurer under third-party liability and recovers ₹1,20,000. It keeps ₹1,15,000 and passes ₹5,000 to Neeta, the deductible she had borne.
faqs: Does subrogation apply to life insurance?

No. Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity; the insurer pays a fixed sum assured regardless of actual loss. So the insurer gets no right to recover from a third party responsible for the death. The family can receive the policy money and still claim compensation from the wrongdoer, for example through a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal.
When does the insurer get subrogation rights?

Subrogation rights arise only after the insurer has paid the claim, and only up to the amount paid. Before payment, the insured holds the rights. Many policies require the insured to sign a subrogation letter at the time of settlement and to avoid any action that could weaken the insurer's recovery.

items.title: Proximate Cause in Insurance: Meaning and Examples
items.description: Proximate cause is the active, efficient cause that sets off the chain of events leading to a loss. Learn how insurers use it to decide claims, with examples.
items.short: Proximate cause is the active and efficient cause that sets in motion a chain of events resulting in a loss, without the intervention of any new independent force.
body: Many losses result from several causes acting together or one after another. To decide whether a claim is covered, insurers and courts identify the dominant, effective cause, not necessarily the one closest in time. If that proximate cause is an insured peril, the claim is payable; if it is an excluded peril, it is not.

When there is an unbroken chain, the first cause is the proximate cause. For example, if an earthquake (excluded under a standard fire policy unless added) causes a fire, the loss is due to the earthquake. When a new, independent cause breaks the chain, the new cause becomes proximate. If insured and excluded perils act concurrently and their effects cannot be separated, the exclusion usually prevails; if they can be separated, the insured part is paid.

In life insurance, proximate cause matters mainly for riders. A basic life policy pays on death from any cause (except specific exclusions like suicide in the first year). But an Accidental Death Benefit rider pays only if an accident was the proximate cause. If a person suffers a heart attack while driving and then crashes, the proximate cause is the heart attack, so the ADB rider may not pay even though the base policy will.
The principle comes from English law (Pawsey v Scottish Union, 1907) and is part of IC-38's core principles alongside utmost good faith, insurable interest and indemnity.
items.example: A godown with stock worth ₹25 lakh is insured under a fire policy that excludes riot. A riot breaks out and rioters set the godown on fire, causing ₹18 lakh of damage. The proximate cause is the riot, an excluded peril, so the claim is rejected. If instead an electrical short circuit had started the fire, an insured cause, the ₹18 lakh loss would be payable, subject to policy terms and average clause.
faqs: Is proximate cause the cause nearest in time to the loss?

Not necessarily. Proximate cause is the dominant, effective cause that started the chain of events, even if other events occurred in between. The last event before the loss may be just a link in the chain. Courts and insurers look at what was truly responsible for the loss.
How does proximate cause apply to accident riders?

An accident rider pays only if an accident is the proximate cause of death or disability. If illness caused the event, such as a stroke causing a fall, the rider may not pay. The basic life cover still pays on death from any cause, subject to standard exclusions like suicide within the first year.

items.title: Term Insurance Meaning: How a Term Plan Works, Example
items.description: Term insurance is pure life cover for a fixed period at low premium, paying the nominee only on death within the term. Learn types, features and an example.
items.short: Term insurance is a pure protection life insurance plan that pays the sum assured to the nominee if the life assured dies during the policy term, with no payout on survival.
body: A term plan covers a fixed period, such as 20, 30 or 40 years, or up to an age like 70 or 85. Because there is no savings or maturity component, almost the entire premium goes towards the cost of risk cover. This makes term insurance the cheapest way to buy a large life cover, often several times cheaper than an endowment plan for the same sum assured.

Variants include: level term (sum assured stays the same); increasing term (cover rises each year to offset inflation); decreasing term, also called mortgage redemption insurance, where cover falls with an outstanding loan; and term with return of premium (TROP), which refunds premiums on survival but costs much more. Death benefit can be paid as a lump sum, monthly income, or a mix.

Underwriting is stricter for large covers: medical tests, income proof and disclosure of habits. Premiums are fixed at entry for the whole term, so buying younger locks in a lower rate. Riders like accidental death, critical illness and waiver of premium can be added.

Common confusion: people often see 'no return on survival' as money wasted. The premium buys protection, much like motor or fire insurance. Another misunderstanding is that term plans don't pay for death by illness; they do, subject to standard exclusions like suicide within the first 12 months, where only a limited refund applies.
items.example: Rohit, 28, a non-smoker earning ₹10 lakh a year, buys a ₹1 crore term plan for 35 years at about ₹11,500 a year. For the same premium, an endowment plan might give a sum assured of only around ₹4 to 5 lakh. If Rohit dies in year 12, his nominee receives ₹1 crore. If he survives to age 63, the policy ends with no payout, and the total premium paid of ₹4,02,500 bought 35 years of protection.
faqs: What happens if I outlive my term insurance policy?

In a pure term plan, nothing is paid if you survive the term; the policy simply ends. In a term with return of premium plan, the premiums paid (excluding taxes and certain charges) are refunded at maturity. Return of premium plans cost significantly more for the same sum assured.
Does term insurance cover death due to illness?

Yes. A term plan covers death due to illness, accident or natural causes during the policy term, subject to exclusions mentioned in the policy, such as suicide within the first 12 months. Accurate disclosure of health conditions at the proposal stage is important to avoid problems at claim time.

items.title: Endowment Policy Meaning: Features, Bonus and Example
items.description: An endowment policy pays the sum assured on death during the term or on survival to maturity, plus bonuses. Learn how it works, with-profit vs non-profit.
items.short: An endowment policy is a life insurance plan that pays the sum assured, along with any bonuses, either on the death of the life assured during the term or on survival to the end of the term.
body: Endowment plans combine protection and savings. Part of the premium covers the life risk and the rest builds a fund, invested mainly in government securities and bonds by the insurer. Because the insurer pays in both situations, death or survival, premiums are much higher than for term insurance with the same sum assured.

With-profit (participating) endowment plans share in the insurer's surplus through bonuses. Reversionary bonuses, declared yearly as a rate per ₹1,000 of sum assured, are added to the policy and paid with the sum assured at maturity or on death. A final or terminal bonus may also be paid at the end. Once declared, reversionary bonuses are guaranteed. Without-profit (non-participating) plans pay only guaranteed amounts, sometimes as guaranteed additions.

Variants include money-back plans (which pay a part of the sum assured at intervals during the term), double endowment and joint life endowment. Policies acquire surrender and paid-up values after the minimum period, and policy loans are available.

For IC-38, remember: endowment = death benefit + survival benefit. The trade-off is lower life cover for the premium and modest returns, so they suit people who value guaranteed, disciplined savings with some cover. Compare the cover needed with a term plan before choosing.
items.example: Sunita buys a 20-year with-profit endowment policy with a sum assured of ₹5 lakh at an annual premium of ₹24,000. If the insurer declares an average reversionary bonus of ₹45 per ₹1,000 each year, annual bonus = 5,00,000/1,000 × 45 = ₹22,500, totalling ₹4,50,000 over 20 years. At maturity she could receive ₹5,00,000 + ₹4,50,000 plus any final bonus, against premiums of ₹4,80,000. If she dies in year 8, her nominee gets ₹5,00,000 + bonuses accrued to date (₹1,80,000).
faqs: What is the difference between an endowment plan and a term plan?

A term plan pays only on death within the term and nothing on survival, so its premium is low. An endowment plan pays on death or on survival to maturity, so it costs much more for the same cover. Term plans focus on protection; endowment plans combine protection with savings.
Are bonuses in an endowment policy guaranteed?

Bonuses are not guaranteed in advance; the insurer declares them each year based on its surplus and investment experience. However, once a reversionary bonus is declared and attached to the policy, it cannot be taken away and becomes payable along with the sum assured at maturity or on death.

items.title: ULIP Meaning: Unit Linked Insurance Plan Charges and Lock-in
items.description: A ULIP combines life cover with market-linked investment in units. Learn ULIP charges, the 5-year lock-in, switching, NAV and how fund value is calculated.
items.short: A Unit Linked Insurance Plan is a life insurance policy in which part of the premium buys life cover and the rest is invested in market-linked funds chosen by the policyholder, in the form of units.
body: ULIPs are regulated by IRDAI, not SEBI. After deducting charges, the premium buys units in funds such as equity, debt, balanced or liquid funds, at the fund's Net Asset Value (NAV). The fund value at any time = number of units × current NAV. The investment risk is borne by the policyholder, which IRDAI requires insurers to state clearly.

Main charges: premium allocation charge (deducted upfront from each premium), policy administration charge, mortality charge (the cost of life cover, deducted by cancelling units monthly), fund management charge (capped by IRDAI at 1.35% a year), and switching, partial withdrawal and discontinuance charges. Since 2010, IRDAI caps the total reduction in yield, making modern ULIPs cheaper than earlier versions.

ULIPs have a lock-in of five years. If premiums stop within the lock-in, the fund moves to a discontinued policy fund, earning a minimum guaranteed rate, and is paid out only after the lock-in ends, minus a capped discontinuance charge. After lock-in, partial withdrawals are allowed. Policyholders can switch between funds, often a few times a year free.

Death benefit is typically the higher of the sum assured (subject to a minimum multiple of annual premium under IRDAI rules) or the fund value. Common mistake: comparing ULIP returns directly with a mutual fund without accounting for mortality and other charges.
items.example: Asha pays a ₹1,00,000 annual ULIP premium. The allocation charge is 4%, so ₹96,000 is invested. With the equity fund NAV at ₹24, she gets 96,000/24 = 4,000 units. Monthly mortality and admin charges cancel, say, 40 units over the year, leaving 3,960 units. If NAV rises to ₹26.40 by year-end, fund value = 3,960 × 26.40 = ₹1,04,544. If she had stopped paying in year 3, her fund would move to the discontinued fund until year 5.
faqs: Who regulates ULIPs in India?

ULIPs are life insurance products and are regulated by IRDAI under the Insurance Act and IRDAI product regulations. A 2010 government ordinance, later an Act, settled a dispute between SEBI and IRDAI by confirming that ULIPs fall under IRDAI's jurisdiction, even though they invest in market-linked funds.
Can I withdraw money from a ULIP before five years?

No. ULIPs have a mandatory five-year lock-in. If you surrender or stop paying within this period, your fund value, minus a capped discontinuance charge, moves to a discontinued policy fund and is paid only after the fifth policy year. Partial withdrawals are allowed only after the lock-in.

items.title: Claim Settlement Ratio (CSR): Meaning, Formula, Use
items.description: Claim settlement ratio shows the share of claims an insurer settles out of claims received. Learn the formula, by number vs amount, and how to read it wisely.
items.short: Claim settlement ratio is the percentage of claims an insurer settles out of the total claims it receives in a year, used as an indicator of its claim-paying record.
body: Formula: CSR = Claims settled ÷ (Claims received during the year + Claims pending at the start of the year) × 100. Many reports simplify this to claims settled ÷ total claims for decision. IRDAI publishes insurer-wise data on death claims in its annual report, and insurers disclose it in public disclosures.

There are two versions. CSR by number counts policies, so a small claim and a large one each count as one. CSR by amount uses the value of claims settled. An insurer may have a high CSR by number but a lower one by amount if it rejects or delays a few very large claims, so looking at both gives a better picture. Repudiation ratio (claims rejected as a share of claims decided) and pending claims are also published.

Timelines matter too. IRDAI regulations set limits for settling claims after all documents are received, with tighter limits introduced by the 2024 master circular, such as settlement within 15 days for death claims not needing investigation and completion of investigation within 45 days. Delays beyond limits attract interest payable to the claimant. Check IRDAI rules (as of 2026).

Common misconception: a 99% CSR does not guarantee that your claim will be paid. Most rejections happen due to non-disclosure of material facts, lapsed policies or excluded causes. Accurate disclosure and keeping the policy in force matter more than small differences in CSR.
items.example: In a year, an insurer had 1,200 death claims pending at the start and received 18,800 new claims, total 20,000. It paid 19,500, rejected 300 and 200 remain pending. CSR by number = 19,500/20,000 = 97.5%. By amount, if claims totalled ₹1,600 crore and ₹1,480 crore was paid, CSR by amount = 92.5%. The gap suggests some large claims were rejected or are pending.
faqs: Where can I find an insurer's claim settlement ratio?

IRDAI publishes insurer-wise claim data, including settlement ratios by number and amount, in its annual report. Insurers also publish claim data in their public disclosures on their websites. Use the latest available year and compare insurers of similar size and product mix.
What is the difference between CSR by number and by amount?

CSR by number shows the share of claims settled counted as individual policies. CSR by amount shows the share of total claim value paid. A large gap between the two may indicate that bigger claims face more rejections or delays, which matters most to buyers of high cover.

items.term: IRDAI (Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India)
items.title: What is IRDAI? Insurance Regulator in India: Role and Powers
items.description: IRDAI regulates and develops India's insurance sector under the IRDA Act 1999. Learn its structure, powers over insurers and agents, and policyholder role.
items.short: IRDAI is the statutory regulator of India's insurance sector, set up under the IRDA Act, 1999, to protect policyholders and to regulate, promote and ensure orderly growth of insurance.
body: The Malhotra Committee (1993-94) recommended opening insurance to private players and creating an independent regulator. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999 established the authority, which began work in April 2000. It was later renamed IRDAI. Its head office is in Hyderabad.

The authority has a chairperson, up to five whole-time members and up to four part-time members, appointed by the Central Government. Its functions under Section 14 of the IRDA Act include: registering insurers and renewing, modifying or cancelling registrations; protecting policyholder interests in matters like nomination, assignment, surrender value and claim settlement; specifying qualifications, code of conduct and training for agents and intermediaries; regulating investment of insurance funds; supervising solvency margins; and adjudicating disputes between insurers and intermediaries.

IRDAI regulates life insurers, general and health insurers, reinsurers, insurance brokers, corporate agents, web aggregators, surveyors and third-party administrators (TPAs). It approves products through its product regulations, sets the IC-38 examination standard for agents through the insurance institute, and runs the Bima Bharosa grievance portal.

In recent years, IRDAI has pursued 'Insurance for All by 2047', replacing many rules with principle-based regulations and master circulars in 2024, raising the FDI cap in insurance, and launching initiatives such as Bima Sugam, a digital insurance marketplace.
items.example: A policyholder's death claim of ₹25 lakh is pending for 45 days after all documents were submitted. Her husband first complains to the insurer's grievance officer. Receiving no response in the time allowed, he registers the complaint on IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal, which tracks it with the insurer. If the matter is still unresolved, he can approach the Insurance Ombudsman for claims up to ₹50 lakh. IRDAI itself does not decide individual claim amounts.
faqs: Where is IRDAI headquartered and who appoints its members?

IRDAI's head office is in Hyderabad, Telangana. The chairperson and members, up to five whole-time and four part-time, are appointed by the Central Government from persons with expertise in life insurance, general insurance, actuarial science, finance, economics, law, accountancy or administration.
Does IRDAI settle individual insurance claims?

No. IRDAI regulates insurers and intermediaries and monitors grievances through its Bima Bharosa system, but it does not adjudicate individual claim disputes. For a claim dispute, a policyholder can approach the insurer's grievance cell, then the Insurance Ombudsman for amounts within its limit, or a consumer commission or court.

items.title: Insurance Ombudsman: How to Complain, Limits, Timelines
items.description: The Insurance Ombudsman resolves policyholder complaints against insurers free of cost. Learn eligibility, the ₹50 lakh limit, timelines and the process.
items.short: The Insurance Ombudsman is an independent, cost-free forum where individual policyholders can resolve complaints against insurers, brokers and agents without going to court.
body: The scheme was created by the Redressal of Public Grievances Rules, 1998, and is now governed by the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017, amended in 2021. The Council for Insurance Ombudsmen administers ombudsman offices across India, each covering a territory. Ombudsmen are typically retired senior officials from insurance, civil services or judicial backgrounds.

Who can complain and about what: individuals, including sole proprietors and micro enterprises in some cases, can complain about delays in claim settlement, partial or total repudiation, disputes over premium, policy terms, mis-selling, non-issue of policy and other service deficiencies. The 2021 amendment extended jurisdiction to insurance brokers and agents, and allowed online complaints and video hearings.

Conditions: the complainant must first complain to the insurer. If the insurer rejects it, does not reply within 30 days, or the reply is unsatisfactory, the policyholder may approach the Ombudsman within one year of the insurer's reply. The claim must be within ₹50 lakh including expenses, and the matter must not be pending before a court or consumer forum.

The Ombudsman first tries mediation; if that fails, it passes an award, ideally within three months of receiving all requirements. The award is binding on the insurer, which must comply within 30 days, but not on the policyholder, who can still go to a consumer commission or court if unhappy. There is no fee. Limits are as of 2026; check the CIO website.
items.example: Rakesh's health insurer pays only ₹1.4 lakh of his ₹3.2 lakh hospitalisation bill, citing a room rent limit. He complains to the insurer's grievance officer on 2 May; the insurer upholds its decision on 25 May. Rakesh files with the Insurance Ombudsman in July, well within one year. After a video hearing, the Ombudsman finds the room-rent clause wrongly applied and awards an additional ₹1.35 lakh. The insurer must pay within 30 days.
faqs: Is the Insurance Ombudsman's award binding?

The award is binding on the insurer, which must comply within 30 days of receiving the policyholder's acceptance. It is not binding on the policyholder. If the complainant is not satisfied, they can reject the award and approach a consumer commission, civil court or other forum.
What is the maximum claim the Insurance Ombudsman can handle?

Under the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, the Ombudsman can decide complaints where the amount claimed, including expenses, does not exceed ₹50 lakh. Larger disputes must go to consumer commissions or civil courts. Check the Council for Insurance Ombudsmen website for any revision of the limit.

items.title: Co-payment in Health Insurance: Meaning and Example
items.description: Co-payment is the fixed share of each admissible health claim that the policyholder pays. Learn how co-pay differs from a deductible, with a worked example.
items.short: Co-payment is a cost-sharing clause in health insurance under which the policyholder pays a fixed percentage of every admissible claim, and the insurer pays the rest.
body: With a 20% co-pay, the insured bears 20% of each eligible claim amount and the insurer pays 80%, up to the sum insured. Insurers use co-payment to reduce premiums and discourage unnecessary or inflated claims, since the insured has a stake in every rupee spent.

Co-pay is common in policies for senior citizens, in group policies, for treatment in higher-cost cities (zone-based co-pay), for treatment at non-network hospitals, and sometimes for specific illnesses. Some policies allow buyers to opt for a voluntary co-pay to lower the premium. IRDAI requires co-payment terms to be clearly disclosed in the policy schedule and customer information sheet.

Co-payment differs from a deductible. A deductible is a fixed amount, say the first ₹25,000 per year, that the insured pays before the insurer pays anything. Co-pay is a percentage that applies to every claim regardless of size. A policy can have both. Co-pay is also different from sub-limits, such as caps on room rent or specific procedures, which limit what the insurer pays for particular items.

Exam and buyer tip: co-pay usually applies after other deductions. First, non-payable items (like some consumables) and sub-limit excesses are removed to arrive at the admissible amount; then the co-pay percentage is applied. So the insured's actual share is often larger than the co-pay percentage of the total bill.
items.example: Mr Iyer, 66, has a ₹5 lakh senior citizen policy with 20% co-pay. His hospital bill is ₹2,50,000, of which ₹10,000 is non-payable consumables. Admissible amount = ₹2,40,000. Co-pay = 20% × 2,40,000 = ₹48,000. The insurer pays ₹1,92,000. Mr Iyer pays ₹48,000 + ₹10,000 = ₹58,000, which is 23.2% of the total bill, more than the 20% headline co-pay.
faqs: What is the difference between co-payment and deductible?

A deductible is a fixed amount the insured pays first, before the insurer starts paying, often annually. Co-payment is a percentage of every admissible claim that the insured shares. With a ₹20,000 deductible, small claims may not be paid at all; with 10% co-pay, the insurer pays 90% of every admissible claim.
Why do senior citizen health policies usually have co-payment?

Older people have a higher probability and cost of hospitalisation, which would make premiums very high. Co-payment lowers the insurer's cost per claim, keeping premiums more affordable, and encourages careful use of healthcare. Some insurers offer senior plans without co-pay at a higher premium.

items.title: No Claim Bonus (NCB): Motor and Health Insurance Rules
items.description: No claim bonus rewards a claim-free year with a premium discount in motor insurance or a higher sum insured in health. Learn NCB slabs, transfer and lapse.
items.short: No claim bonus is a reward given by an insurer for a claim-free policy year, either as a discount on the next renewal premium in motor insurance or as an increase in sum insured in health insurance.
body: In motor insurance, NCB is a discount on the own-damage part of the premium, not on third-party liability premium. It builds up over consecutive claim-free years in standard slabs: 20% after one year, 25% after two, 35% after three, 45% after four and 50% after five or more claim-free years. A single own-damage claim usually resets the NCB to zero at the next renewal, unless an NCB protection add-on is bought.

NCB belongs to the insured person, not the vehicle. When you sell a car, you can transfer the NCB to your new vehicle by obtaining an NCB certificate or retention letter, and the policy on the old car is transferred to the buyer without NCB. If the policy is not renewed within 90 days of expiry, the accumulated NCB is lost.

In health insurance, NCB is usually called cumulative bonus. For each claim-free year, the sum insured increases by a percentage, such as 10% to 50% a year, up to a cap, at no extra premium. Under IRDAI health regulations, if a claim is made, the bonus can be reduced in the next year at the same rate it was added, but the base sum insured is protected.
Common mistakes: assuming NCB applies on the full motor premium, or that changing insurers resets NCB; it does not, as long as you renew on time.
items.example: Pooja's car has an own-damage premium of ₹12,000 and third-party premium of ₹3,400. After four claim-free years her NCB is 45%, so the OD premium becomes 12,000 × 55% = ₹6,600, total ₹10,000 (before taxes). If she makes a ₹15,000 repair claim this year, next year's NCB drops to 0% and the OD premium returns to about ₹12,000, raising her premium by ₹5,400, more than a third of the claim value. She may choose to pay a small repair herself.
faqs: Can I transfer my car's NCB to a new car?

Yes. NCB is attached to the owner, not the vehicle. When you sell your old car, ask the insurer for an NCB certificate or retention letter and present it when insuring your new vehicle. The new policy will then carry the same NCB percentage, usually valid if used within three years of the old policy's expiry.
What happens to NCB if I renew my policy late?

In motor insurance, if you renew within 90 days after the policy expires, the NCB is retained, though the vehicle may need inspection and is not covered during the gap. Beyond 90 days, the accumulated NCB lapses and you start again from zero. Timely renewal is the simplest way to keep it.

items.title: Underwriting in Insurance: Meaning, Process and Decisions
items.description: Underwriting is how an insurer assesses a proposal's risk and decides whether to accept it and at what premium. Learn hazards, decisions and an example.
items.short: Underwriting is the process by which an insurer evaluates the risk in a proposal and decides whether to accept it, on what terms and at what premium.
body: Underwriting protects insurers from adverse selection, the tendency of people with higher risk to seek more insurance. Without it, premiums would have to rise for everyone. The underwriter classifies each proposer into a risk class so that people with similar risks pay similar premiums.

In life insurance, underwriters consider medical factors (age, height and weight, blood pressure, diabetes, past illnesses, family history), lifestyle (smoking, alcohol, hazardous hobbies), occupation, and financial factors (income versus sum assured, existing cover). Sources include the proposal form, the agent's confidential report, medical examination and reports, and financial documents. Non-medical underwriting is allowed for smaller covers and younger ages, relying on the declarations alone.

Hazards are of two kinds: physical hazard, arising from the subject itself (a chronic illness, or a factory storing chemicals), and moral hazard, arising from the attitude or behaviour of the insured (carelessness, dishonesty). Underwriting decisions include: accept at standard rates; accept with extra premium (rating up); accept with exclusions, lien or reduced cover; postpone (for example, until recovery from a recent surgery); or decline.

In general insurance, underwriters look at the property's construction, location, safety measures and claims history. Underwriting at the field level begins with the agent, who is often called the primary underwriter because he first sees the proposer.
items.example: Two 40-year-olds apply for a ₹1 crore term plan. Asha is healthy and a non-smoker, so she is accepted at the standard premium of ₹18,000. Vinod has controlled diabetes and a BMI of 33. The underwriter accepts him with a 50% extra premium, so he pays ₹27,000. A third applicant, who had heart surgery three months ago, is postponed for a year so that his recovery can be assessed before cover is offered.
faqs: Why is the agent called the primary underwriter?

The agent meets the proposer face to face and sees their lifestyle, health signs, occupation and financial standing before anyone at the insurer does. The agent's confidential report and the information collected at this stage form the base of the insurer's risk assessment, which is why IC-38 calls the agent the primary underwriter.
What is the difference between physical and moral hazard?

Physical hazard relates to tangible features of the risk, such as a person's medical condition or a building's construction material. Moral hazard relates to the insured's behaviour or intentions, such as carelessness after being insured or a temptation to make false claims. Underwriters assess both before accepting a proposal.

items.title: Reinsurance Meaning: Treaty vs Facultative, India Example
items.description: Reinsurance is insurance bought by insurers to share large risks with other insurers. Learn treaty vs facultative, proportional cover, GIC Re and an example.
items.short: Reinsurance is the arrangement by which an insurance company transfers part of the risks it has insured to another insurer, called the reinsurer, in exchange for a share of the premium.
body: Reinsurance is often described as insurance for insurers. The original insurer, called the ceding company or cedant, keeps the portion it can safely bear (its retention) and passes on the rest. This lets insurers accept large risks, such as a refinery, an airline fleet or a ₹50 crore life cover, stabilise their results against catastrophes like floods and cyclones, and free up capital.

Two main methods: facultative reinsurance is arranged risk by risk, where the reinsurer can accept or decline each proposal, suitable for unusually large or special risks. Treaty reinsurance is an agreement covering a whole class of business automatically. Treaties may be proportional, such as quota share (a fixed percentage of every risk) or surplus (amounts above retention), or non-proportional, such as excess of loss, where the reinsurer pays losses above a set threshold.

In India, GIC Re (General Insurance Corporation of India) is the national reinsurer. Indian insurers historically had to cede a fixed percentage of general business to GIC Re as obligatory cession, a requirement that has been reduced over time. Foreign reinsurers operate through branches in India and in GIFT City under IRDAI's reinsurance regulations. Check IRDAI rules for current cession requirements (as of 2026).
The policyholder's contract is only with the original insurer. Even if a reinsurer fails to pay, the insurer must still pay the policyholder in full.
items.example: A general insurer issues a fire policy of ₹200 crore on a factory but its retention limit is ₹20 crore. It keeps ₹20 crore as its retention and places the other ₹180 crore with reinsurers through quota share and surplus treaties. So it bears 10% of the risk and keeps 10% of the premium, plus the commission reinsurers pay it on ceded business. If a fire causes a ₹50 crore loss, the insurer pays the full ₹50 crore to the factory and recovers ₹45 crore from reinsurers.
faqs: Does a policyholder have any contract with the reinsurer?

No. The policyholder's contract is only with the original insurer. The reinsurance contract is between the insurer and the reinsurer. If a reinsurer defaults, the insurer must still settle the policyholder's claim fully and then pursue the reinsurer separately.
What is the difference between treaty and facultative reinsurance?

Treaty reinsurance automatically covers all risks in an agreed class of business under pre-set terms, so the reinsurer cannot reject individual risks. Facultative reinsurance is negotiated case by case for individual risks, and the reinsurer can accept or decline each one. Facultative is used for unusual or very large exposures.

items.title: Section 45 Insurance Act: 3-Year Rule on Policy Disputes
items.description: Section 45 bars a life insurer from questioning a policy after 3 years. Learn what it allows within 3 years, fraud vs non-disclosure and a worked example.
items.short: Section 45 of the Insurance Act, 1938 says no life insurance policy can be called in question on any ground after three years from the date of issue, risk commencement, revival or rider addition, whichever is later.
body: Section 45 protects policyholders and their families from claims being rejected many years later over old statements in the proposal form. It was substantially rewritten by the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015. The three years are counted from the date of the policy, the date of commencement of risk, the date of revival, or the date of the rider, whichever is latest.

Within three years, the insurer may repudiate a policy on the ground of fraud, or on the ground of misstatement or suppression of a material fact. It must communicate the grounds and materials for its decision in writing to the insured, nominee or legal representatives. If the repudiation is for fraud, the insurer need not refund the premium. If it is for innocent non-disclosure without fraud, the premiums collected until the date of repudiation must be refunded within 90 days.

Defences against a fraud allegation are built in: the insurer cannot repudiate for fraud if the policyholder proves that the misstatement was true to the best of their knowledge and belief with no deliberate intention to suppress, or that it was not within their knowledge. Silence is not fraud unless there was a duty to speak.

Two practical points: Section 45 does not prevent the insurer from asking for proof of age at any time and adjusting terms if age was misstated. And revival restarts the three-year clock only for statements made at revival.
items.example: Meera buys a ₹50 lakh term plan on 1 July 2022 without disclosing a thyroid condition. Case 1: she dies on 1 March 2025, within three years; the insurer finds the non-disclosure, judges it material but not fraudulent, and repudiates, refunding premiums of ₹31,500 paid so far within 90 days. Case 2: she dies on 15 August 2025, more than three years after issue; the insurer cannot question the policy on any ground and must pay ₹50 lakh.
faqs: Can an insurer reject a claim after three years for non-disclosure?

No. Under Section 45 as amended in 2015, a life insurance policy cannot be called in question on any ground, including fraud or non-disclosure, after three years from the latest of the policy issue, risk commencement, revival or rider date. The insurer can, however, adjust benefits if age was misstated.
Does reviving a lapsed policy restart the three-year period?

Yes, for statements made at the time of revival. If the policyholder makes a false or incomplete health declaration while reviving, the insurer can question the policy on that basis within three years from the revival date. Statements in the original proposal remain protected if more than three years have passed since issue.
